maintopic: RAILWAY ACCOMMODATION IN THE NORTHWEST.
RAILWAY ACCOMMODATION IN THE NORTHWEST.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I wish to read to the House a telegram dated May 19th, which I received on Friday morning iast following the adjournment. It is addressed to myself, and reads as follows :-
Regina, N.W.T., May 19.
Walter Scott, M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Last night at 8 o'clock the first work train crossed the valley at Lumsden, and this morning three special trains with bridge gangs and construction material left here for Saskatoon. Superintendent Brownlee certainly did remarkable work in getting the Lumsden break repaired much quicker than anybody had expected.
To-morrow (Friday) first passenger through train will go out and the road opened for settlers' effects and seed grain. Great relief.

maintopic: P. M. BREDT,

speechtext:
After the discussion which has taken place in the House within recent weeks upon the conditions which were brought about through the traffic tie-up on the Prince Albert Branch Railway, it is perhaps only fair that the House should be made acquainted with the fact that the western management of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are entitled to great credit for the vigour with which they have taken measures to repair that extensive break ; and to Superintendent Brownlee, who, I am advised personally supervised the work of repair at Lumsden, and worked almost incessantly night and day until the break was repaired, a special recognition is due. While on my feet, I wish to read to the House a very brief statement upon the subject made by second Vice-president Whyte, of Winnipeg. I taken this from the Winnipeg 1 Free Press ' of Saturday last:
A large deputation of wholesale men, members of the board of trade, interviewed Mr. W. Whyte yesterday in response to a request from Prince Albert Board of Trade. The deputation urged strongly on Mr. Whyte that no delay should be allowed in opening the Prince Albert branch for business, as considerable freight absolutely required by the settlers and shipped from Winnipeg in March, has not yet reached its destination at points along that line. In some cases cars of goods, such as seeders, will be positively unsaleable this year, and will have to be carried for twelve months.
Mr. Whyte stated that the line was now open for delivery of freight to the broken bridge over the Saskatchewan, and that the neces-

maintopic: P. M. BREDT,
speechtext:
sary material and machinery was now on the ground and "work "would he vigorously prosecuted. Officials expect the bridge to be ready for business in ten days. The company are ferrying from six to eight carloads a day at Saskatoon, settler's effects being given first preference. Mr. Whyte stated he had prepared a list of improvements, such as raising the grade at low points, that would have to be made by the owners of the road and in case the owning company failed to do this, the Canadian Pacifie Railway would hand the road over to the owners for operating themselves.
This statement, of course, requires no further comment.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.

speechtext: House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the third reading of Bill (No. 72), to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few evenings ago I gave notice to the House that I intended to move an amendment to the Bill which is now before the House ; and in the few remarks I have to make, I intend to speak as closely to the question as possible. A year ago, when this measure was before the House, I placed myself on record as opposed to the contract made by the government with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. I also had the pleasure of making a few remarks in op-, position to the measure. I was and still am in favour of the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to the Georgian bay, and also to the Northwest and Pacific ocean. The government would then be in a position to control for all time the freight rates from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and vice versa. I believe it would be in the interest of the whole of the people of Canada to have government ownership of railways in this country, just as many other countries have it. The amended Bill which has been under discussion this session has postponed the government ownership of railways for fifty years longer than the Bill of last year. Under that Bill the Grand Trunk Pacific Company had the privilege of running the proposed road for fifty years. The amended Bill of this year gives them the privilege of running it for fifty years longer if they see fit ; so that this company will have control of this road for the next hundred years, and the public ownership of railroads will be put off for that length of time.
Before saying anything directly upon the question of the Alien Labour Law, I wish to state that I am in favour of a good immigration policy. I am in favour of bringing good, honest people from European countries to settle in our Northwest and to assist in developing the immense territories we have there. On the 13th of May last, we had a discussion in this House brought on by the hon. Minister of Labour (Sir William Mu-lock) regarding .the complaint of the civil

engineers of Canada that preference was given to foreign engineers on the surveys of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I do not know why the hon. minister chose that particular evening to bring on the discussion, unless he wished to bring it on before a thin House. On Friday evening a great many members as a rule, leave for home, and the hon. minister probably thought fit to take advantage of their absence and thus avoid the full discussion which would have taken place had the subject come up on another day. The hon. the leader of the opposition had made a motion asking for copies of letters and documents from the civil engineers, and the Minister of Labour knew that he had not done his duty when he failed to investigate the complaints which these men had laid before the government, and was anxious to avoid discussion as much ns .passible. But if the debate turned out disastrous to himself and his party, as it did, he has only himself to blame. In Ids attempt at defence, he tried to draw a herring across the trail by making a most unjustifiable and unfair attack on the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The course of that hon. gentleman on the labour question needs no defence, if there is a man who has stood by the labouring classes, it is the hon. member for West Toronto. He has not played to the galleries, as is the custom of the Minister of Labour, and as that minister did the other night when tie read the letters from the civil engineers. For many years that hon. gentleman was in this House before he became a minister of the Crown, and in ail these years he cannot show that he ever had anything to say in the interests of the labouring classes. But take the record of the hon. memker for West Toronto, and yon will find that for over thirty years he has been continuously identified with the labour	interests	of this	country.	Hegave his	energetic	aid to	the men tovindicate their right to organize themselves into	unions,	and that at a	timewhen the	political	friends	of the	Minister of Labour and his party were trying to crush the unions by sending men to jail, including the hon. member for West Toronto himself ; and never under any circumstances, was he known to have received one cent of money from any labour union for his services.
When the Minister of Labour charges my hon. friend with having made his living out of a labour commission, he makes a charge which he must know to be thoroughly unwarranted in fact. My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has had conferred upon him by the citizens of Toronto the highest honour at their command. In that city, where he is best known, he has had the honour of being elected mayor during four consecutive years ; in the Ontario legislature, he represented the city of Toronto during eight years ; and at the last election 109
he polled the largest vote obtained by anv candidate elected to this House and obtained the largest majority gained by any hon. member in the province of Ontario. I venture to assert that my hon. friend, who is a printer, and who knows the needs of the working men of this country, has done more to alleviate their condition since he has been a member of this House than the Minister of Labour and the cabinet which he belongs to ever dreamt of accomplishing. Does the Minister of Labour forget that it was the hon. member for West Toronto who brought up in this House year after year, the question of remuneration of the civil service ? Does he forget that it was my hon. friend who was the first to raise his voice in the interests of the trackmen of the Grand Trunk Railway, who were getting from ninety cents to one dollar per day ? And if the government have appointed an officer to examine into and report on the causes of all railway accidents in which life is lost, who was it that impressed on the government the necessity of doing this ? It was my hon. friend ; it was he who first brought that matter to the attention of this House. In connection with the civil engineers, the Minister of Labour tried to defend the work he had done. Last session the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) openly declared that the great majority of the civil engineers employed to make the surveys of the Grand Trunk Railway in the Northwest were Americans and aliens. Yet still the Minister of Labour has the assurance to ask what hon. members on this side have done for the workingmen. But, Mr. Speaker, it is not the duty of this side of the House to carry out the laws. It is to the government that duty is entrusted, and when this matter was brought up before the Minister of Labour a year ago, he should have taken some action to have an investigation and find out whether the report made by my hon. friend from North Victoria was correct. The hon. Finance Minister who was then acting Minister of Railways declared in the House a few evenings ago that he wrote to Mr. Hays that these complaints had been made and that Mr. Hays denied that they had any foundation. The Minister of Railways, or the acting Minister of Railways, even spoke to Mr. Hays, and Mr. Hays again denied that they had any aliens employed on the surveys. I bring these matters up to show that the Minister of Labour must have known practically the charges that were made, yet he took no action until the 19th of April to investigate whether they were true or false. Last January the Canadian Association of Civil Engineers wrote to different members of the cabinet, making these charges, ana in March they offered to the government to prove their truth, if the government would give them a chance to can witnesses. But all the minister did was write to the

Grand Trunk to find out wfietfier tney were employing aliens or not.
The Grand Trunk did not deny the charge, but sought to disarm criticism. A concern that will bring aliens into Canada under contract to labour, if it is willing to break the law in this respect, will be quite ready to make excuses for its action. In one of the communications from Mr. Hays written, not to the Minister of Labour (Sir William Muloclr), but to the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) Mr. Hays acknowledges the fact that aliens have been brought in to be employed in the service of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. That letter stated that 96 per cent of these employees were Canadians, and the others were Americans. Here in this very letter is all the proof required by the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulockl if he really desired to put the law into effect. The other evening the Minister of Labour inquired tauntingly what bon. members on this side of the House had done to bring this matter to the attention of the House and the government. Well, Mr. Speaker, the House met on 10th March, and on the 15th March, the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) gave notice of motion for a return as follows :
For a return showing :-

On March 17th the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) gave notice of this inquiry :
Have any protests been received from or on behalf of the Society of Canadian Civil Engineers, or from any person or persons, respecting the employment of aliens on the surveys being made in connection with the proposed National Transcontinental Railway ; and if so, from whom were such protests received, and when were they presented to the government ?	.
The Minister of Labour must have known all this, as these complaints were laid before every member of the cabinet; and surely, they tell each other what letters they receive -sometimes at any rate. On March 22nd the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) gave notice of inquiry :
1.	Is the government aware that survey parties are at work along the route of the proposed Transcontinental Railway between Winnipeg and Quebec ?
2.	Are these parties employed by the government or by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company ?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
3.	If by the railway company, is there any understanding that the government will adopt the surveys, and pay the expenses incurred in making them ?
4.	In case the cost will ultimately be met by the government, is it not possible to take some steps to remedy the grievances, if such exist, as set out in the petition received by the Minister of Railways from the Dominion Institute of Amalgamated Engineers ?
5.	Have any such steps been taken ?
Still, nothing was done. On the 23rd of March the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) gave notice of the following question :
1.	What answer, if any, has been made to the protest received by the government on the 16th March, 1904, from the Dominion Institute ot Amalgamated Engineers, respecting the employment of aliens on the surveys being made in connection with the National Transcontinental Railway ?
2.	Have any instructions been issued by the Department of Labour ? And if so, on what date, and of what nature, respecting the eif-forcement of the Alien Labour Law by the deporting of aliens, alleged to be employed on the surveys being made in connection with the National Transcontinental Railway ?
3.	Is it the intention of the government, in its new agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to provide for the employment of British subjects, as surveyors and engineers, in the work of surveying and construction of the new Transcontinental Railway ?
And so we see that day after day, this matter was brought before the Minister of Labour and still no action was taken by him. On the oth April the House began the discussion of the motion to go into committee on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Bill, and on the following day the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) gave notice of the following question :
1.	Has the Minister of Labour received any communication from Mr. George L. Griffith, ot Winnipeg, provincial secretary for Manitoba of the Dominion of Canada Institute of Amalgamated Engineers, calling attention to the number of aliens employed on the surveys of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and giving the names of aliens employed in connection with such work at Winnipeg and Edmonton ?
2.	When was such communication received ?
3.	Is it the intention of the government to take action upon Mr. Griffith's communication, and to order the deportation of the aliens complained of ?
That, Mr. Speaker, was on Cth April. Xo action whatever was taken upon it. On 11th April the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) gave notice of this inquiry :
1. Has the Minister of Labour received from the Dominion of Canada Institute of Amalgamated Engineers a request for the deportation of the following men, brought into Canada under contract by the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company ?
Then follows the list of names which it it is not necessary that I should read. And the question proceeds :
2.	What reply has been given to the request ?
3.	Has the minister taken any steps to ascertain the total number of men imported under contract from the United States in connection with the survey of the proposed Transcontinental Railway ?
The Minister of Labour did absolutely nothing even after all these inquiries. On 25th April the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) gave notice of motion, and this was the first thing that led the minister to take some action in this matter, for it seems that, after this, at least a communication was addressed to Mr. Hays of the Grand Trunk Railway making inquiry on this subject. The notice of motion given by the leader of the opposition was as follows :
For copies of all letters, correspondence, memorials, petitions and documents, in the possession of the government, relating to the employment, or requesting the employment, by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, of British subjects as engineers in the surveying and construction of the proposed National Transcontinental Railway ; and generally, all correspondence and documents in the possession of the goverment, in any way complaining ot, or protesting against, the employment of aliens as engineers in railway surveying or construction on the line of the proposed National Transcontinental Railway.
On April 27tli the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Ralph Smith) gave notice of motion for return as follows :
For a statement showing the names of all American aliens employed in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific surveys in Canada ; the nature of their employment, and the reasons for their employment, to the exclusion of Canadians. *	|
You will notice. Mr. Speaker, that, in this notice of motion the hon. member for Vancouver takes it for granted-no doubt knowing it to be true-that aliens were being employed by the Grand Trunk Railway in making surveys on this line. I bare a letter here signed on behalf of the Dominion Institute of Amalgamated Engineering, for Manitoba, Northwest Territories and British Columbia to the Minister of Railways, in which the charges are made and reiterated. They also say in this letter that there are any number of civil engineers in Canada out of employment, a great many more than were required by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
Men trained and experienced in railroad engineering work are now employed in subordinate commercial positions here at inferior remuneration, who are anxious to secure engineering work, but could not do so and were compelled to resort to some other means of securing a living and maintaining their families.
If the government will grant us a commission of inquiry with power to take evidence under oath to send for persons and papers and to incur all necessary cost and sit on the investigation Until completed, we will not only 10$H
prove every general statement made but much more.
Later in the letter there is the following quotation from a letter written to the Prime Minister by Mr. Hays :
So far as I can learn, last year ninety-five per cent (95 per cent) of the Grand Trunk Pacific staff were Canadians or British subjects. It is represented that of the entire staff of ninety-four (94) last session, eighty-nine (89) were Canadians.
Discussing this they say :
If this statement be thoroughly and critically examined it can easily be proven to be absolutely untrue, either the Grand Trunk Pacific management are wilfully deceiving your government or the engineering oflieials are wilfully deceiving the management of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
To prove that the statement made by the Grand Trunk Pacific, that out of the entire staff of ninety-four, eighty-nine were Canadians, Is untrue, I herewith give part of the personnel of the Winnipeg and Edmonton divisions alone :

. And several others. All these names were in the possession of the government as engineers from the other side who were brought in here to take the place of our men-our men who are willing to work-our men who are out of employment-but the Minister of Labour would not even make an investigation until a few days ago when lie telegraphed for one of these engineers to come down from Winnipeg when nearly one half of the surveying work in the Northwest had been completed.
In the year 1900, when I first became a member of this House, I had the honour to Introduce a Bill in the interests of labour. What I principally objected to and what the working people of Canada objected to was that while we had a law on our statute-books we bad no provision by which the people most Interested in the enforcement of that law could take

344S
action to secure its enforcement. As the law stood at that time no action could bd taken without the consent of the Attorney General of Canada and X considered it my duty to bring in a Bill which would enable the law to be enforced without any expense by the people who were most interested in its enforcement. I shall read a few lines from ' Hansard ' of the statement I made in this House at that time .
The object of this Bill is to provide a simple way to carry out the law now in force, which was passed in 1897. I do not believe that the mechanics and labourers of this country wish to have high-salaried officers to carry out the Act, if a more simple, efficient and economical way can he found to enforce that law. As it is at present, the Act is entierly in the hands of the government to enforce it, and I do not believe that the government has enforced it in the interest of the labouring class and mechanics of this country. On the other hand, I believe that the officers who were appointed to enforce the law were engaged more for the purpose of keeping the government and the members of the government party out of trouble than of assisting the mechanics and labouring class	 I believe that if the Bill I am now discussing were enacted, the law would be more strictly carried out, and with not one cent of expense. My Bill provides that any person, for instance, any labouring man or mechanic who is interested, should have the power to lay information before two magistrates and so enforce the law. That would not cost the country one cent, for those who are most interested, the mechanics and labouring men, would see that the law is strictly enforced. I myself have quite a number of men in my employ. In my own business I am protected from foreign competition, and I see no reason why the labouring class and mechanics in my employ and in the employ of other manufacturers of this country should not be as well protected from foreign competition as I am, especially as the people to the south of us have a law to the same effect.
Had this Bill been allowed to go through this House we would not have had any discussion of this kind at present. There would have been no aliens working on the Grand Trunk surveys, for the men who are interested, the engineers of this country would have seen that the law as provided in my Bill was enforced, and the carelessness of the Minister of Labour would not have prevented the deportation of these aliens from this country. Unfortunately the Prime Minister refused to allow my Bill to go through. He side-tracked it and brought down a Bill on behalf of the government. This Bill while to a certain extent an improvement on the original Act had the very same objection as the Bill of 1897 ; that is, it put every possible obstacle in the way in order to make it unworkable. Instead of appealing to the Attorney General of the Dominion for the enforcement of the new law it was necessary to apply to the Attorney General of the" province of Ontario for a judge before the matter could be brought before the Mr. CLARE. I claim, Mr. Speaker, that the Alien Labour law as it is at present is a thoroughly political enactment, and that only when party advantages are to be gained is an attempt made to enforce it. In the election in 1900 in the riding of South Waterloo, which I have the honour to represent in this House, the Alien Labour law was put in force promptly by the labour party of the government. Why was it done promptly . Because there was a political party advantage to be gained at that time, and I say

again that it is ouly for political party advantage that the Alien Labour law is put in force. There was a certain firm in the town of Preston which brought in several men from the United States and gave them employment. My opponent in the contest telegraphed to the Labour Department and immediately an officer landed in the town. These people were not written to first to find out whether the statements in regard to them were true or not as were the Grand Trunk people, but a political advantage had to be gained and immediately a man landed there and these men were put out of employment. My opponent was expected to receive the credit for this great good that the Labour Department of Canada had done to the people of Preston. It is in this way that the Labour Department is being used. But I may say that the labouring classes of the good town of Preston saw through the flimsey dodge and gave me a majority of three hundred. The resolution that I intend to move will give the Hon. Minister of Labour power to suspend the restriction of labour on the construction of the road. This is done so as not to retard the completion of the road. It, however, does not give him power to allow alien engineers to make surveys and do engineering work on the road for the following reasons :
1.	We have in abundance of qualified engineers resident in Canada who are British subjects who can do the work. Many of these men are out of employment at present.
2.	Because Canadian engineers would not be likely to discriminate against Canadian contractors and manufacturers in connection with contracts or supplies for the road.
3.	Large numbers of the leading officials of the Grand Trunk Railway are Americans and their interests, sympathies and affiliations are American rather than Canadian.
4 With American engineers in charge of this work it is only natural the interests of their countrymen will not be overlooked.
5. Canadian manufacturers and contractors will be absolutely at the mercy of these alien engineers in the interpretation of the contracts or in the awarding of orders for supplies.	.
0. Because it is absurd that in a great national undertaking the money for the carrying out of which is supplied on the credit of the country, aliens should be appointed and employed to carry out the proposal and Canadians ignored and discriminated against.
These are the reasons for my resolution which I shall close by moving as follows :
In all cases where persons are employed in or in connection with the surveys for or the construction of the said Transcontinental Railway preference shall be given to British subjects by birth or naturalization.
It shall be unlawful to employ any person in or in connection with the surveys for or the construction of the said Transcontinental Railway. or any part thereof who is not a British
subject by birth or naturalization, or who, being an alien, has not for one year immediately preceding such employment been a bona fide resident of Canada.
Provided always that wherever it shall be made to appear to the satisfaction of the Minister of Labour that it is not possible to obtain labour for the construction of the said railway with reasonable despatch owing to the restriction aforesaid with regard to the employment of labourers it shall be lawful for the said minister by order in writing to suspend for such time and on such terms and conditions as may to him seem reasonable in the premises the operation of the said restriction as to employment of labour for construction purposes only. And a copy of such order of suspension shall be forthwith published in the ' Labour Gazette.'
For every violation of any of the provisions of this section the person, partnership, company or corporation violating it shall forfeit a sum not exceeding $1,000, nor less than $50, and a further sum of $50 for each and every day during which such unlawful employment shall continue.
The sums so forfeited may be sued for and recovered as a debt by any person who first bona fide brings his action therefor in any court of competent jurisdiction in which debts of like amount are now recovered.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House will not quarrel with the sentiment expressed in the amendment of my hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare), I believe that I would be voicing the opinion of not only the House but of the country if I were to say, that the prevailing determination of the people of Canada is to protect Canadian labour whenever it is possible to do so. This is not a new question ; in former sessions as during the present session, it has been brought before the attention of the House more than once, and in the course of this debate my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and I think the premier as well, intimated that it was the intention of the government to legislate this session ; not perhaps to the exact tenor of this amendment, but in a much more comprehensive manner. This amendment simply applies to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, including I presume the eastern division which is to be built by the government. So far so good, but why my hon. friend should limit the benefit of a good movement to but one line of railway, I am unable to understand. There are other railways and there are other enterprises which will be built or aided by public money and to which a law of the kind proposed in the amendment, would be equally applicable. If such a measure would be good if applied to the Grand Trunk Pacific, it follows that it would be better if it were more extensive in its scope. Before the labours of this session are ended, my hon. friends opposite will have ample opportunity to discuss a measure that will be far more comprehensive in its general application than would be this proposed

amendment if adopted. It would, therefore, seem inopportune ; unwise in fact to apply a measure of this kind to only one public work. While the government is unable to accept this amendment, I may say that it is because we trust to be able to secure the concurrence of parliament to a much larger measure of usefulness to the working classes of Canada-not only to the working classes, but to others whose services will be required in the operation and construction of public works. As to the charges "made against the Grand Trunk Pacific Company of having already violated either the letter or the spirit-perhaps both-of the Alien Labour Act ; and incidently with regard to my hon. friend's reference to myself ; perhaps it would not be expedient to protract the discussion on this matter by bringing in a subject not germane to the passage of the Bill itself. When, later on in the session, the larger measure which I trust parliament will assent to, comes before us, there will be ample opportunity for my hon. friend (Mr. Clare) to pay attention to me, and to any of my supposed shortcomings. As was said a few days ago, we have a conflict of statements as to the charges against the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have the accusations of those who say that tliei Grand Trunk Pacific has violated the law, and on the other hand we have statements made by the Grand Trunk, partially confessing, partially denying, but up to the present moment unsatisfactory. Since the question was last debated in parliament, further correspondence has taken place between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific, but that correspondence has not resulted in a satisfactory elucidation of the question. The controversy raised is not yet satisfactorily adjusted and the government is of opinion that the charges and the denials of the parties are not sufficient to bring out the facts, but that a more thorough system of inquiry should be resorted to. Accordingly, I have to announce that already the government has directed the issue of a commission to inquire into the truth or otherwise of these charges.

rect in saying that no judicial appointment by this government has received more hearty approbation from the public in general-not merely from those who may be politically in sympathy with us, but also from those who do not always give us their confidence-no judicial appointment I say, has ever been more heartily received by the public of Canada generally, than the appointment of Judge Winchester. He had for twenty years filled a semi-judicial position before he was raised to the high office he now occupies, namely that of senior judge of the great county of York including the city of Toronto. Judge Winchester is the gentleman who is entrusted with the inquiry into these charges and denials. The inquiry will be thorough and the inquiry will be speedy. My hon. friends opposite may perhaps think otherwise, but I can assure them that the government has no purpose to serve by, in the slightest degree, preventing the most thorough inquiry ; and if during the progress of that inquiry any gentleman on the other side, either here or elsewhere, has any suggestions that he thinks would add to the thoroughness of the inquiry, I am sure the most respectful reception will be given to such suggestions. At all events, the very debates that have taken place upon this question warrant legislation in the direction that the government proposes, even if it should happen that the report of the commissioner would not fully sustain the whole of these charges. The government is fully determined to protect Canadian interests, not only in respect to the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway, but with respect to all similar enterprises aided or carried out by the Canadian public. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that I would be justified in prolonging the debate on this subject, and therefore I will say no more at the present moment, except that I trust that when this important measure has passed the House, and when we can give our attention to other matters, one of the earliest measures that will be submitted for consideration, and which will appeal to you for sympathy and support, will be a measure promoted by the government to protect Canadian labour and Canadian interests not merely in the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway, but as to all railways and public works hereafter aided by the public of Canada, either by land, by gift, by guarantee or otherwise. This is not the first occasion on which a question of this nature has arisen in connection with public works. In a contract that was made by this government with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway a clause was included providing substantially for the protection which is now asked in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) has disposed a little hastily of a very important question. It is a very important question for us in the city of Montreal and in the neighbourhood of that great city, *where we have a very large number of working men ; and I think it is our duty to secure for those important classes as much protection as possible in the construction of the great work which we have now under consideration. My hon. friend, I think has made a mistake in saying that the proposer of this amendment should have extended the terms of it to all the railways under constitaction in Canada. It is probable that my hon. friend who has moved this motion in the interest of the working classes and of the engineers of this country has been accustomed to consider, from the language that has fallen from the lips of hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches, that this is essentially a national interest. We have been told that it was essentially an undertaking of a Canadian nature ; and viewing it from that standpoint, I for one consider that as far as possible and under the limitations indicated
in this amendment, since that great work is being executed, thanks to our money or our credit, none but Canadians should be employed in the work of construction. I would go, even further and say that it seems to me that the rolling stock of that great * company should be constihieted exclusively within the limits of the Dominion of Canada. It is being built largely with our money, and why should not that money be spent here, among our working classes, so long as we have everything that is necessary in Canada to furnish the whole of that rolling stock ?
I rose, Mr. Speaker, because I have said that in my part of the country, this amendment must be of intense interest to many, not only of the working classes, but of the educated classes as well. We have in the city of Montreal, as you are no doubt aware, thanks to the munificence of some of our wealthy citizens-one in particular, who is well known-probably the best equipped school of applied science on the continent of America. From that school, which is attached to McGill University, are liurned out every year young men who are most competent in every way to carry out the works referred to in the first part of my hon. friend's motion. We have also side by side with that school, but equipped far more modestly, I regret to say, attached to Laval University, in which Jbe people of my own province take a very great interest, a polytechnic school with excellent professors, who turn out yearly and deliver degrees to a very large number of our French Canadian young men ; and from what I see and have heard, and from the certificates that have been given wherever these young men have been employed, they are admirably fitted for engineering work in connection with this or any other railway. Why should not these young men be employed in preference to aliens ? My hon. friend the mover of this amendment has given the names and addresses of eighteen or twenty engineers who have already been engaged for work on the construction of this new railway. I had expected some explanation in regard to these men from my hon. friend the Minister of Labour. He has not vouchsafed to give us that explanation ; Gut surely the fact that these engineers have been engaged in the United States, and have been brought to this country to begin this work, ought to put us on our guard, and make us as careful as possible for the protection of our own Canadian interests in a matter of this importance. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour has gone so far as to say that under present conditions we require a general law more perfect than that which we have at present in order to exclude alien labour ; but if that is the case, I would ask my hon. friend why that law' has not been introdiuced before now ? Why has my hon. friend not taken the precaution to bring that law down, in order to save us the trouble of making

3455
this amendment ? Then, again, my hon. friend the Minister of Labour lias stated that in the construction of the Crow's Nest Lass Railway there was a clause included in the contract made between the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway, which I have now in my hands, but which I will not read to the House, which clause was intended to protect effectually, as this amendment does protect, our Canadian labourers and engineers.
If the government at that time thought it proper to insert such a clause in its contract regarding the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway-a much less important contract than the present one- what objection can my hon. friend have to similar legislation in this instance ? We have a law against the importation of foreign labour, but, as every one knows, it is not carried out. Every day we read of infractions of it. Scarcely a day passes but in some of our newspapers we have facts which show clearly that our government will not in any way enforce that law. Contrast their laxness in that respect with the vigilance of the American government. The Americans take a very different view of the importation of aliens. Instead of seeking to increase the numbers of their population by any means whatever, they enforce a policy which is rather one of exclusion. No alien, no matter where he comes from, is allowed to enter their national family unless he is found in every way worthy to form part of it ; and if we were to follow a similar policy, we would be all the better off. Let me give the House one or two instances to show the strictness exercised at the American frontier. Since 1891 the Americans have been making their law more and more exclusive every year,, and their efforts culminated in the legislation approved on the 3rd March, 1903, which excludes from the United States not only labourers imported under contract, but every one who might become in any way a burden on the country and be the cause of material or moral deterioration. In volume 9 of the Senate reports of the United States, I find the report of an inquiry held by the foreign immigration commission of the American Senate upon contract labour and alien labour imported into the United States. Amongst other things, I find in that report that from the year 1892 to the year 1901, out of a total of 3,615,163 persons, who sought admission into the United States, there were debarred 20,031 ; and as being in violation of a law, which has existed since 1891, against the importation of contract labour, 6,119 aliens were prevented entering the United States. Since a couple of years the American government has greatly increased the number of officers employed by it along the Canadian border, to an extent of nearly 4,000 miles, to prevent any Canadian labour from entering the United States. Mr. Watchorne, superintendent of the American Immigration ser-Mr. MONK.
vice in the Dominion, has given the American government a very full report of his operations in that regard, and I find that in the year 1902, there were 275 aliens rejected as contract labourers and in the following year the rejections on that score numbered 1,903. I am quoting from the annual report of the Commissioner General of Immigration for the fiscal year ending 30th June, 1903. There is another statement of alien labourers excluded from the United States ; and last year the total from our country prevented from entering the United States amounted to 431. How many have we excluded who attempted to come into Canada from the United States ? As a matter of fact, our law excluding contract labour is not put into effect ; and until we can come to some more satisfactory arrangement with the American authorities regarding this exclusion of our labouring classes, it is our duty to apply to them the same treatment which they apply to us. I believe that at present, when these important works are being undertaken, we should see that Canadian engineers are given the preference. Look at our large cities, how many of our workingmen would find useful employment if protected by the amendment we are now submitting ? I have a report of the committee of inquiry held by the American Senate, and I was surprised to see in that report the deposition given under oath by Mr. Richmond, who has been for some time president of the Industrial Commission of the United States. Questioned by members of the commission, Mr. Richmond placed at the enormous figure of 70,000 French Canadians a year, those who left the province of Quebec to work in the United States.
It seems almost incredible, but that is what he deposes under oath, and as a result of most careful investigation made by himself and his assistants. Why do not we, in the construction of this great national work, endeavour, by the protective amendment introduced by my hon. friend (Mr. Clare) to keep here within our own territory and occupied on our own national works, these people, many of whom, as stated in the deposition, remain in the United States and never return to Canada ? These are working men, men who do not belong to the class of engineers to which I have already referred, but they are entitled to our fullest consideration. And let me, before I resume my seat, point out to my hou. friend the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) that this amendment goes, and necessarily goes, beyond the law *which we have at present. It is quite possible that these seventeen or twenty engineers referred to by my hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) have come into Canadian territory without violation of any law whatever. What our law, as well as the law of the United States, forbids, is the importation of aliens under contract for the execution of labour. These engineers may have come

into Canada without violation of the general law. They may have come here hoping to obtain employment and without any special inducement, and, arriving here, have secured this employment quite legitimately. But my hon. friend's amendment goes deeper into the question and is more patriotic. By the terms of that amendment none but Canadians can be employed as engineers or in any way on the construction of this railway unless those who are constructing it can satisfy the government that they are obliged to have recourse to the help of aliens. It seems to me that, under the circumstances and in view of the character of the work and the amount of money we are spending upon it, the amendment is justified and should be adopted.

It is not my intention to follow my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) through all his argument. But I wish to point out one slight difference between that argument and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare). My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has made a very strong plea in favour of the employment of Canadian labour. With the object of his argument I agree entirely, though I must say that, when it comes to the employment of scientific men for the construction of public works there is a further word to be said. Though I join heartily with my hon. friend in the desire that, as far as possible, preference be given to Canadian engineers, yet we must admit that if we made a stringent law that none but Canadian engineers be employed in the construction of railways we might be deprived, to our own injury, of the services of high grade engineers from other countries, who would not only be required for certain parts of the work, but whose employment might be actually a benefit to Canadian engineers. I do not think, therefore, that we should make a law so stringent that it would forbid either the Canadian government or a railway company or other corporations engaged in large scientific or industrial development, bringing from foreign countries for the time being first-class engineers who have made deeper and more special studies than may have been made in this country, or who have had experience in the construction of works of a specially difficult character that have not been constructed in Canada. But I will not dispute with my hon. friend on that point. He advocates the adoption of the amendment of the hon. member for South Waterloo in order to give encouragement to Canadian labour and Canadian engineering. But the amendment of the hon. member for South Waterloo is much broader. It says :
In all cases where persons are employed in or in connection with the surveys for or the construction of the said Transcontinental Railway, preference shall be given to British subjects by birth or naturalization.
This amendment, if adopted, would leave the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company free to employ engineers from England, Scotland, Ireland or any other part of the British Empire.

Perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) is aware that the most difficult parts of the Canadian Pacific construction

was carried out under two Canadian engineers, if I am not mistaken. One is the engineer who resigned from the company not long ago, and the other, Mr. Peterson. And he was assisted in that work by a French gentleman of Montreal with whom my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) is no doubt acquainted, but whose name I have for the moment forgotten. speechtext:
I do not dispute at all that some Canadian engineers are to be found equal to any to be found in any other part of the world. I simply lay it down at the beginning that, perhaps, we should not go too far in our restrictive laws as to engineering and other work. It is not that we have not the engineers we want, but that if we do not make the restrictive law to apply to all people but Canadians, then, we should have no. restriction at all. What I have suggested is that it might be dangerous to do so. The time might come when two or three engineers of great eminence may be sought by a railway company to superintend the building of a specially difficult section and they being employed elsewhere, it might be advantageous to the whole country to have the railway company left free to apply to the United States, Great Britain or any other country to secure the engineering skill required. But I say that if we adopt the principle of protection to Canadian work then it should be restricted to Canadian work. That is the principle I have laid down, and if my hon. friend would be logical, he would apply to bis friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) and ask him to make his amendment a case of Canadian protection. When it comes to a question of protection to manufacturers we are Canadians and I think we are right to be Canadians. When it comes to a question, which is a more doubtful one, of protecting Canadian labour and Canadian engineering, then let our legislation be sincere and be a measure purely and simply Canadian, for Canadian work and Canadian engineering.
The quotation that has been made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) showing the application of the American Alien Labour law is not, I think, a reason why we should follow their example. I have a great deal of admiration for the Americans, but I am not prepared to take all my lessons from the United States. For the greater part of their past national life, the Americans made the mistake that perhaps we ourselves are making, of not only opening their doors, but of calling loudly for foreigners to come in and people their land. 1 think they made a mistake ; and I shall never forget the words of warning that were uttered to me by a statesman of the United States, whom I cannot now name, because he is still in public life, but whom I Mr. MONK.
had the pleasure of meeting several times in Washington five years ago. He said : 'You have the great advantage on your side of the border of being able to look back at' the past life of our country, the United States, so as to avoid the mistakes that we have made and to take advantage of the good laws and the good measures we have adopted. If we have made a mistake it has been that at one time we called loudly for foreign-labour and foreign settlement to come into this country ; and if to-day the American nation is one which it is not easy to govern, that condition comes from the fact that we have been anxious to fill up our country too soon. Now we have gone to the other extreme, and have adopted restricting laws (hat certainly are not worthy of a civilized nation. You should take advantage of our past experience, and not be so anxious to import foreigners. In this way you will not be obliged later on to adopt restricting laws, as we have been forced to do.'
We are not obliged, as the United States now are, to guard every port of entry into this country in order to prevent a large amount of undesirable immigration coming in. So far as the highest class of immigrants are concerned, scientific men and engineers, my hon. friends may be content on one point, that the first-class engineers will not come, either from the United States or from other countries, for a number of years, because they make a much more satisfactory and profitable living in other countries. Therefore, I do not think it will be necessary to adopt the restricting laws that have been adopted in the United States, both as regards the highest immigration and ordinary immigration. But if we have to adopt such restricting laws, if they are imposed on us, let us be frank and let them be laws of restriction and laws of real protection for Canadian labour, and for Canadian labour only.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised to hear the hon. the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) make the statement a few moments ago that when this country gave a few millions, about ?f3,000,000 bonus to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the purpose of building the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, the government at that time took a great deal of credit to themselves for having introduced a clause into the Act, or the agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway, that the company should employ nothing but Canadian labour in building that road. Yet here to-day the government are spending fifty times the amount of the subsidy which they gave to the Canadian Pacific Railway in constructing that road, but the Minister of Labour is put up by his colleagues in the government to call upon their supporters to vote down an amendment which gives protection to Canadian labour in building this road, upon which $150,000,000 is to be expended. The Minister of Labour, who should be the first

to say, either if he has to break away from this government, if the premier and his following, save and except the Minister of Labour, propose voting down the amendment-who should be the first one to stand up in the interests of the labouring men of Canada and say : I shall support the amend ment of the hon. gentleman.
The alien labour movement in Canada has a history, and the Minister of Labour is largely connected with that history. I had the honour, in the year 1890, of introducing the first Alien Labour Bill in this House. If you will look at the Journals of the House for 1890, you will find a report of a sub-committee to whom was referred the Bill which I then introduced. The report is as follows :
Your committee find, on examination, that this Bill is similar in all respects to a Bill passed by the Congress of the United States in 1885, and amended by that body in 1886.
Your committee have had before them witnesses from different points along the frontier, and And from their evidence (copy of which is annexed hereto) that the American Alien Labour law has been enforced in such a way as to compel many of our people to relinquish their employment in the United States, or to remove with their families, and reside there permanently, while citizens of the United States are permitted to work in Canada every day, and to return to their homes on the American side of the frontier at night, without interference from the Canadian authorities.
Your committee recommend that the attention of the authorities at "Washington be directed to the oppressive application to Canadians of the American Alien Labour law, and to allow of such representation being made, and to afford time for its due consideration, recommend that further consideration of this Bill be postponed until next session ; and if some suitable measure for granting relief to Canadians from the grievance complained of, be not passed in the interval by the American authorities, then your committee recommend that a Bill dealing with this question be introduced next session, and taken into consideration.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
(Signed) GEO. TAYLOR, Chairman.
That report was submitted to the House and adopted1. I do not intend reading al! the evidence that was attached to that report, but I shall read the evidence given by Mr. William Wainwright, of the Grand Trunk Railway.

speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me to make my speech he can then get up and make his. The American government withdrew the application of the Alien Labour law as far as it affected the Thousand Islands and the River St. Lawrence. There was a common application of the American and Canadian laws between Kingston and Ogdensburg. That was one concession they made between 1890 and 1896. However, the negotiations were not satisfactory to the Canadian government Mr. TAYLOR.
and I introduced my Bill again the last session that the Conservative party were in power. The Bill did not go through. The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in making his appeal previous to the elections of 1896, issued his manifesto and said: Put us in power and we will introduce an alien labour law word for word with the American law. The people put him in power and he put up the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) to forestall the Bill that I had introduced. That hon. gentleman introduced a copy of my Bill word for word save and except the clause that made the Bill effective. That was left out. The Bills are on file up stairs where they can be found. Both of these Bills were referred to a special committee to report on. The Hon. Sir Louis Davies, now on the Supreme Court bench, was a member of that committee and I remember very well the fights that took place when these Bills were before the committee. The government had a majority on that committee and they carried their point. They introduced their Bill without the penal clause attached to it. The result is that instead of having an alien labour law, as the right hon. Prime Minister had promised word for word with the American law, you cannot enforce the Canadian law without moving the whole government. Before a prosecution can be taken it must have the approval of the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General of Canada. No person can put the law into effect, whereas, in the United States all you have to do is to make a complaint before a customs officer or a justice of the peace and the law is enforced. The Bill I introduced had a similar clause in it but this government struck that out when they introduced their Bill. The Conservative * members upon that committee made a minority report in which it was pointed out that if the Bill were passed in the form recommended by the majority it would prove ineffective just as it has proved ineffective. I see by the Auditor General's Report that the hon. Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) spent $44,000 of the people's money last year -making believe that he was enforcing the Alien Labour, law.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
