speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
No, but the hon. gentleman pretended that he was doing something for labour and he has spent of the people's money $44,000. What has he accomplished by this expenditure for labour ? When an amendment is proposed by my hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare! in the interest of labour he opposes it and calls upon his supporters to vote it down. Here is a sample of how he spent $44,000 of the peo-1 pie's money :

D. J. O'Donoghue, a special officer, trip to Ldvis anti St. John, Aug. 2 to 10, $34.40 ; trip to RiviOre Ouelle and Halifax, Aug. 12 to 18, $32.60.
And other trips making in ail for trips, tips and car service, $663.60. This gentleman who draws a salary of some $1,500 is employed in making these special trips. He is a special organizer for the Grit party ; that is all he is and every man who is named in this Auditor General's Report as participating in this expenditure of $44,000 is simply an organizer for the Grit party and not working in the interest of labour at all. I could read their names, but at a later stage I intend to deal with the whole subject of trips and tips. This lion, gentleman, having spent $41,000 for political purposes purely and not in the interest of labour at all, gets up and calls upon his supporters behind him to vote down an amendment which is the first step that has ever been taken to protect Canadian labour. He calls upon his supporters to vote it down and no doubt they will do it. Some of them will try to dodge the question, but, [DOT]when it is proposed to expend $150,000,000 upon a transcontinental railway he says that the labour employed may be Chinese labour, or any other kind of labour and that we will not put a clause in the contract as we did in the ease of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but we will make it applicable to all railways. This Grand Trunk Pacific Bill will go into effect right away, and I am informed that a great majority of the engineers employed on the line today are brought over from the United States by Mr. Hays, and these gentlemen are figuring so as to have their reports favourable to the contractors who may tender for this work, being Americans. I hope thef supporters of the hon. gentleman will not take his advice and vote down the first motion to protect Canadian labour that has been offered in connection with this measure.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I have listened with a good deal of pleasure to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor). In view of the past history of Canada, it ill becomes Conservative members to get up in this House and impute motives such as they have imputed to the Liberal party. It does not lie in their mouths to accuse the Liberals in this respect, when they themselves have been the greatest sinners in the matter of allowing alien labour to be employed on Canadian national works. It is a recognized fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway, which to-day we ai'e all proud of, was built almost entirely by Americans and Chinese.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Rosser the chief engineer was an American, and he afterwards became I suppose a British subject ; George Brackett the contractor was an American citizen from Minneapolis. Mr. Stickney the general manager was an American, and he was superseded by Sir Wm. Van Horne who we all know was an American. Mr. J. F. Egan the general superintendent was an American ; he was afterwards in charge of construction, and I am told by a man who was working there at the time, that Canadian road masters were jAit out of business and Americans put in their places. The labourers to work on the Canadian Pacific Railway were brought over in carloads from Wisconsin and from the Mormon settlement in Utah, and in boat loads from China. Major Rogers who located Rogers Pass was an American, and I suppose no worse pass could have been selected. The Canadian Pacific Railway have great difficulty with it to-day, while on the other hand we all know that Canadian engineers located the Yellow Head Pass down the North Thompson river, which would have been an infinitely better route for the Canadian Pacific Railway to have adopted. The question to-day with us is however, not to recriminate about the past, but to recognize the mistakes that have been made and address ourselves to the task of providing that such mistakes shall not Occur again. I care not what political party introduced alien labour legislation, or what party did not ; the fact remains to-day, that the Canadian Alien Labour law, which I understand is taken almost word for word from the American Act, is not found to be workable. We have had a case in British Columbia, in which an engineering firm inserted an advertisement in the Seattle papers inviting workmen to come over to take the place of others who had gone on strike. The proprietors of this establishment were proceeded against by the labour people of the city of Vancouver, but the decision of the police magistrate, Mr. Williams, was against the labour union. An appeal was taken to the Supreme Court, and Mr. Justice Duff, one of our leading judges in British Columbia gave a decision which is so important that it is worth while reading to the House. It is as follows :
Mr. Justice Duff delivered his judgment yesterday morning in the suit of Downie vs. The Vancouver Engineering Works, which is of considerable importance in that it shows that the Alien Labour Act is unworkable. The judgment in full is as follows :

maintopic: IN THE SUPREME COURT OP BRITISH COLUMBIA.

speechtext:
Before Duff, J.
Vancouver-, May 17th, 1904.
In the matter of the dismissal of an information under the Alien Labour Act, styled Downie vs. Vancouver Engineering Works, in re the importation of Cornelle Mesere, contrary to the provisions of the Act, being an appeal from the decision of the police magistrate of Vancouver.

maintopic: Duff, J.

speechtext:
This is a case stated for the opinion of the court by Mr. Williams, the police magistrate of Vancouver, on the hearing of any information charging the Vancouver Engineering Works Company, Limited, with an infraction of the first section of chap. 60 and 61, Victoria, Statutes of Canada, which section reads as follows :
' From and after the passing of this Act, it shall be unlawful for any person, company, partnership or corporation in any manner to prepay the transportation, or in any way to assist or encourage the importation or immigration of any alien or foreigner into Canada under contract or agreement, parole or special, expressed or implied, made previous to the importation or immigration of such alien or foreigner to perform labour or service of any kind in Canada.'
In support of the charge, it was proved that the accused had caused to be inserted in a newspaper published in Seattle, in the State of Washington, an advertisement in the following terms :
' Wanted-First-class	machinists. Apply
Vancouver Engineering Works, Limited, Vancouver, B.C.'
The magistrate Jias found as a fact that the accused company was responsible for the publication of. this advertisement. Chap. 13 of 1 Edward 7 Statutes of Canada, section 4 amended the 8th section of the last mentioned Act by substituting therefor the following, provision :	* It shall be deemed a violation of this
Act for any person, partnership, company, or corporation to assist or encourage the importation or immigration of any person who resides in or as a citizen of any foreign country to which this Act applies, by promise of employment through advertisement printed or published in such foreign country and any such person coming to this country in consequence of such advertisement shall be treated as coming under contract as contemplated by this Act, and the penalties by this Act imposed shall be applicable to such,' and then follows a proviso which is not here material.
The question submitted for the opinion of this court is :	' Does the advertisement, thei
terms of which I have read, contain a promise of employment. It is, I think, an invitation to apply for employment and nothing more. It was urged on behalf of the prosecution that the second clause of the 8th section of the Act as amended, in effect declares that where you have an advertisement published in a newspaper in a foreign country, which induces a citizen or resident of that country to come into Canada with the expectation of obtaining employment here, you have a contract within the meaning of the Act, but the advertisement referred to in the second clause of that section is plainly, I think, an advertisement of the character dealt with in the first clause of the same section, and obviously an advertisement dealt with in the first clause of the section is an advertisement containing a promise of employment. That argument, therefore, I think, begs the question. It is said that the enactment must be construed with reference to the practice of persons designing to obtain employees by means of a notice published in the newspapers, and that it is not in accordance with such practice that such notice should contain either an express promise of employment or any words implying or suggesting such a promise more forcibly than the words in question here. Now, I have not the materials before me to form a Mr. MACPHERSON.
judgment upon the point of fact, but assuming the fact, am I also to set up an assumed policy of the legislature, namely the intention to prohibit invitations to apply for employment as well as promises to employ, and in conformity with this assumed policy to assign a forced or unusual meaning to the terms which the legislature itself has selected to set forth its design. Parliament, not usually parsimonious of language, has in this case employed a precise phrase, and I must look to the words themselves for the policy of the legislature, not elsewhere. Nor can I agree with the argument of Mr. Bird that on this construction the amendment of 1901 adds nothing to the Act of 1897. Obviously the Act of 1897 reached those cases only in which the immigration was preceded by a completed contract of service. Before the passing of that Act, the Federal courts of the United States had more than once held that an enactment of congress framed in similar terms did not prohibit an agreement arising from offer and acceptance, where the immigration of the employees itself constituted or was an essential ingredient in the acceptance of the offer of employment. It is plain that the principle of these decisions would have no application to the limited class of cases embraced within the scope of the amendment of 1901, and to that extent that amendment has enlarged the restrictive provisions of the Act.
It was strongly pressed upon me that the legislation thus construed imposes no effective restraint upon the importation of foreign labour in times of industrial stress or emergency and that this result is altogether alien to the spirit and to the design which prompted these enactments. If so, the remedy must, I think be sought elsewhere. In ne case, least of all in a penal proceeding, can I press the words of the legislature^ beyond their fair and natural sense. The question submitted by the case will be answered in accordance with this opinion. With regard to^ costs, as the point now raised for the first time, is not without difficulty, I think it is not a case for costs.
In this decision Mr. Justice Duff holds that the Canadian Alien Labour law, which was framed after the law of the United States, is not workable. It is a well known fact that the amendment of 1901 to the Alien Labour law was brought in at the instigation of the Trades and Labour Council of the city of Rossland. A strike was on there, and they thought the amendment would make the law more workable. I believe the Act was more workable before that amendment was brought in. But the fact stares us in the face that people are allowed under our laws to bring in almost any one they wish. I do not think it is right or fair that persons should be brought in who will not become citizens of our country, to compete with our own citizens, or with persons who will become citizens. I would open the doors wide to men who will come in with their wives and families, and become citizens and make homes for themselves ; but I think it is a mistake to allow any one else to come in. I am glad to say that we have in power to-day a government who are alive to the interests of the labouring people of our country, as no previous government has been, and I trust that we

shall have an Act brought in covering, not merely one isolated case, but all cases. The labouring people of Canada have been handicapped by the fact that whenever a big undertaking has been started in our country, hordes of Americans have been allowed to come in and take the cream, leaving to our people the skimnnilk. But I believe the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific should be, as it is meant to be, iu the interest of the whole people of Canada. If we cannot get men enough in Canada to build it, then it will be time enough for us to go outside.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Is not that exactly what the amendment of the bon. member for South Waterloo proposes ?

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext:
In my estimation, the amendment only goes half way. I am not criticising my hon. friend's remarks at all. I am speaking as a Canadian, and I believe that I am voicing the sentiments of the people of Vancouver and of the province of British Columbia. In that province we have had a curse which the people of eastern Canada have never had-a yellow plague, a blight on our country, which has done us more harm than can be undone by the good which any government can do for many years to come ; and if we are to be alive to the interest of our people, we must be alive to this question. The first thing done for us by any government was when this government imposed a tax of $500 a head on the Chinese coming into our country. We fought for that measure for a long time. If the Canadian Pacific Railway had not been built, we would not have had those people in our country. I am not saying anything derogatory to the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is a grand institution, which has done a great deal for British Columbia and for Canada. But ho corporation, be it the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk Pacific, should be allowed to bring in a horde of aliens, whether Chinese, Japanese, Polanders or any others, whom we cannot expect to become citizens of our country. Therefore, T wish to see a general Act brought in by the government covering this whole ease. I do not want to see an Act applicable only to one railway or to one corporation, but an Act applicable to all. We have seen the evil of this thing in the province of British Columbia, where we have 35.000 Orientals and 165,000 white people. Not one of these Orientals is on the voters' list or is contributing to the support of churches or schools, or anything else that goes to make a nation.
I speak for the labouring men of the province of British Columbia, when I say that if an Alien Labour Act is to be brought in that will be workable and cover the whole ground, it must be such an Act that when our own men are turned out of employment, on account of a strike or other labour trouble, they will have some redress for their griev
ances, instead of seeing aliens brought in to take their places.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? He said that he believ [DOT] ed the amendment made to the Alien Labour law in 1901 was made at the suggestion of the Rossland Trades and Labour Council. What authority had the hon. gentleman for making that statement ?

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: My authority is Mr. Foley, who was a member of the Rossland Trades and Labour Council at that time. He was my opponent during the last election, and he said he was the cause of having that amendment made. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Ralph Smith) is not here to day, or he would back up my assertion.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext:
The remarks of the hon. gentleman reminded me of a voter in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, who does my opponent all the harm lie possibly can : he invariably speaks for him, and invariably votes against him. Our hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Macpherson) has spoken to the resolution of the hon. member for South Waterloo and intends to vote against it, thus doing it all the harm he possibly can. The hon. gentleman's parallel of the Canadian Pacific Railway will not hold. He has stated that the Chinamen would not have been in Vancouver if the Canadian Pacific Railway had not been there. Sir, there would have been no Vancouver if the Canadian Pacific Railway had not been there. Our friend himself would not have any constituency to represent if the Canadian Pacific Railway had not been built, and I dare say he would have been still in the eastern part of this country, or wherever he happened to be born, occupying a more humble position than he does in Vancouver.
Mi-. MACPHERSON. The hon. gentleman does not wish, of course, to misquote what I said, apart from the context. I said all these undertakings permitted the possibility of these people coming in.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext:
The words of the hon. gentleman were just as I quoted them ; I took them dow'n at the time. Furthermore, the parallel of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, drawn by the Minister of Labour^will not hold. Medical officers were employed on construction works in this country long before the Crow's Nest Pass iniquity was perpetrated. The hon. minister suggests that that iniquity would have been ameliorated had their law been in force.
I want to tell the hon. Minister of Labour, what he must know, that the conditions pertaining to the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway were a scandal to the Dominion of Canada. Men were treated there worse than horses should have been treated. Men died and were thrown on the dumps by contractors-not

Chinese alone, but stalwart young white men of Canada. When their friends sought for years to find out what had become of them, all they could find was that they had died on the works. And that was done under the auspices of the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: I had not the honour of being Minister of Labour at that time.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Had not the honour! Had not the dishonour, I would say, if allowed to express it. The question, to my mind, in connection with this engineering business is not one of an alien labour law. This great National Transcontinental Railway has been heralded all over the country as running from a Canadian seaport to a Canadian seaport, all the way on Canadian soil, and engineered by a Canadian company, when, as a matter of fact, not one solitary man on the engineering staff is a Canadian, but are all brought in from the United States, and not one of them is a man of any particular standing. Those who are conversant -with engineering work know that Canada has to-day a large number of engineers as competent as any in the United States. Take Mr. McLeod, the engineer who laid out and superintended the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway. That work is reputed one of the finest pieces of civil engineering on the continent of America, and it was planned and superintended by a young Canadian boy who comes from the county I have the honour to represent.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Is Mr. McLeod Out of a job ?

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Were these gentlemen brought in from the United States engaged simply because they were out of jobs ? If so. I regret exceedingly that the Grand Trunk Railway have been going around picking up the off-scourings of the United States-picking up engineers here and there wherever they could find one out of a job.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Is Mr. McLeod out of a job at present ?	.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: He is not, but if he were offered the salary these gentlemen are likely to get-$15,000 to $30,000 a year when incompetent officers get $10,000 a year-I have not the slightest doubt that Mr. McLeod would have been delighted to accept the position, of chief engineer of the road.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know that Mr. McLeod has resigned the position he holds, and does he know or not whether Mr. McLeod has been offered a position on the Grand Trunk Pacific ?

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext:
He has not been offered the position of chief engineer, nor has it been offered to any other Canadian engineer. No Canadian engineer has been Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
offered directly or indirectly even the second position on the Grand Trunk Pacific.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: My information is that even if Mr. McLeod were offered a position on the Grand Trunk Pacific with an increased salary, hs wohjld not take it and give up the one he has.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has no evidence of his statement. A.11 he lias is mere rumour. We have, in addition to the McGill University and the Laval University, the Royal Military College of Canada, which has turned out some first-class engineers. We have also the School of Practical Science in Toronto, for a young institution, has turned out a very large number of competent engineers. It is an anomalous condition of affairs when Canadian engineers, graduates from such institutions- particularly graduates from the government owned institution, the Royal Military College-should be passed over simply to give offices to Americans who happen to be out of employment. There is another matter to which I wish to refer. Our hon. friend, the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) always bristles up whenever anything British happens to be mentioned. Whenever the subject of British connections comes up, his hair stands out like bristles on a prickly porcupine and he jumps into the arena and shouts for Canada. Let me tell him that Canada is part and parcel of the British Empire and intends remaining so. Let me tell him that the British empire gives to our university graduates and young engineers from our Royal Military College positions in her service. Let me point out that many of the finest officers in the British navy are Canadians, and that in the British civil service position after position is open to young Canadian engineers and officers trained in our universities'. Britain reciprocates with Canada in these respects, but the United States will not reciprocate with _<us in any sense. Just imagine a Canadian getting a position as engineer on the staff of the United States government. The thing would be preposterous. Any one travelling over the border to the United States will see an American alien labour officer passing through the train and inspecting every passenger; and if there is a young fellow going through who has not a return ticket, he puts him through a careful examination to ascertain whether he is going in under contract, and if he does not furnish evidence that he is an ordinary traveller, he is deported at once. I remember when the Minister of Labour was one of those responsible for having placed this bogus Alien Labour law on the statutes, under which it is impossible for us to turn a labour alien out of the country. I had no intention of speaking further on this subject than to point out to our good friend from Labelle that it would be well for him to look at the matter seriously and realize that Canada is going to remain part

and parcel of the British empire, and in matters of .appointment to office and legislation generally, I have no doubt that the bonds of the union will be made a little tighter and the colony and the mother country drawn closer together rather than further apart.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: I have a copy of the decision read by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Macpherson). It is a decision of Mr. Justice Duff, of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, delivered only the 17th of this month, which completely nullifies one of the principal sections in the Alien Labour law.

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext: Which section ?

maintopic: Duff, J.
speechtext:
Section 8. That suggests to me the advisability of including in this Bill a section or clause similar to that proposed by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Clare). It seems to me necessary that something should be put into the Bill to bring to the mind of the company, as well as the judges, our intention to have the Alien Labour law applied in this case. The effect of the Alien Labour law has been nullified by the judgment. The hon. member for Burrard was not in the House in 1901 when that law was amended by a Bill bro*ught in by the First Minister, and the introduction of that amendment I believe was due to a strike in British Columbia, during which the miners were brought in wholesale from the United States, in reply to advertisements printed in all the mining camps of the United States. It was asked by the Trade and Labour Congress that a clause should be drawn which would make the inserting of an advertisement in an American paper evidence of a contract. In introducing this clause 8 to the House, in 1901, the First Minister said :
The labour organizations would insist-and this is a proposition, which I think perfectly reasonable-that the Act should be so framed, so constructed and so interpreted as to make it impossible, when there is a dispute between employers of labour and their employees, when there is a strike on or any difficulty of that kind, to advertise in the United States, and' thereby get a supply of labour for the market here while the dispute is going on.
That is exactly what was done in Vancouver last year. When the strike was on the company advertised in the Seattle papers, the advertisement being in these words, as already read to the House :
Wanted. - First-class machinists. Apply Vancouver Engineering Works, Ltd., Vancouver, B.C.
This is the very kind of thing that we tried to make illegal and to subject to a fine. And, on the seventeenth of this month, the judge of the Supreme Court nullified that section, in effect, by declaring that that kind of advertisement is not the kind of advertisement that we intended to specify, because,, 110
as a matter of fact, it does not promise employment. Now, that is the way our Alien Labour law has been interpreted. Ordinarily, I should accept as perfectly satisfactory the statement that has been made to-day by the Minister of Labour that a general Bill will be introduced to cover these matters. Under ordinary conditions I would assume that this is the proper thing to do. And perhaps it is. But the very fact of this decision in British Columbia makes it imperative, in my opinion to state in this Bill that we are now passing, which is for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk, exactly what we mean, so as to impress it upon these companies that we are bound to give protection to Canadian labour, in preference, at all events, to alien and United States labour. Now, I notice that the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock), this afternoon has told to us that the complaints that have been made by a certain interest as regards the employment of engineers and surveyors' have not been satisfactorily explained, and that a commission is to be appointed or has been appointed to inquire into the matter. So far no good. But we had at one time, an alien labour officer of the department. What has become of him ? We were under the impression that these eases were investigated, that we had an officer whose salary we were paying, and I suppose are paying yet, called the Alien Labour Law Officer. Surely it would be better, cheaper and quicker to have that officer investigate these complaints as they arise, instead of letting them accumulate and then taking them in a bunch to be investigated by a judge.
During this debate the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has seen fit to attack the Labour Department to some extent, and one of the officials of that department, D. J. O'Donoghue, he charges with being nothing but a Grit heeler and organizer. Now I have not taken part in any party stripes, in this House or this country, and do not intend to do so. But I want to advise the hon. member for South Leeds that it is not possible to make political capital iu this country by attacking the character of D. J. O'Donoghue. That man has a record for forty years as a labour student and labour worker. Speaking for practically all the labour people, not only those and his frffends but his enemies, I can say that they have confidence in D. J. O'Donoghue, and all regard his record as a credit to the labour movement in Canada. If the government have many men in their employ so keenly alive to the interests in their charge, so conscientious in the performance of their duties, they are indeed fortunate. I repeat, you cannot make political capital in Canada by attacking the character of D. J. O'Donoghue.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.

speechtext: House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the third reading of Bill (No. 72) to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act and the proposed motion of Mr. Clare in amendment thereto.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken I would like to say a few words on the amendment introduced by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare). This amendment is further evidence, if further evidence was needed, of the abiding interest that hon. gentleman takes in the welfare of Canadian workingmen. It is not the first time that he has placed the toilers of this country under obligations to him by introducing legislation to promote their best interests. If the Bill introduced by the hon. member

in 1901 to amend tlie then existing Alien Labour Act had become law the difficulties with which we have had to contend from that time up to the present would not have been encountered. The amendments which he proposed were simple and would have been effective; they woiuld have provided the simple machinery necessary in order that those aggrieved by reason of the importation of alien labour could take advantage of the law and by summons proceed against the violators before police magistrates in cities and towns throughout the country. The amendment which the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) endeavoured to have made to the Alien Labour law having been set aside by order of hon. gentlemen opposite, a further attempt was made when the Prime Minister in 1901 introduced his Bill amending the Alien Labour Act. to simplify its provisions by providing machinery similar to that contemplated under the Bill introduced by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare). But that attempt met with the steady united opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite, and although the opinion was ventured from this side of the House that without some such amendment as was then suggested the Alien Labour Act even as amended by the Prime Minister would become a dead letter, yet hon. gentlemen opposite turned a deaf ear to the suggestions and recommendations, and from 1901 up to the present time attention has been drawn again and again through newspaper reports to the fact that the Alien Labour law as we have it on the statute-book to-day is to all intents and purposes a dead letter. My hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) has taken, in my htumble judgment, the best possible way to deal with this matter. He has striven from his place in the House to make the Alien Labour law effective. He has failed in those attempts, but by the amendment which he has now introduced he proposes to go a step further than has been taken in any law which has been passed by the Canadian parliament in the direction of securing an efficient Alien Labour law. I congratulate the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clare) on the position he has assumed. His amendment is so fair and so reasonable that I am astonished that any opposition is made to it.
It is a singular fact, Mr. Speaker, that while every hon. gentleman opposite who has spoken on the amendment of n>y non. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) has approved of it practically, every one of them proposes to vote against it and for what reason ? Because they allege that the government propose to introduce some general legislation upon this subject. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is no reason why we should not give favourable consideration to the legislation of the government when that legislation is submitted to us. For my part 1 shall be glad, if I have the pleasure of being present in the House when the legislation
conies down, to support the hands of the Hon. the Minister of Labour if the legislation is in the direction which he intimated this afternoon. But in the meantime this most important measure Which has been before parliament for weeks, and which is now in its last stages before the House, ought not to be permitted to pass beyond our purview without our making it clear beyond per-adventure and beyond the decision of the courts of this country that if the people of Canada are to provide by the credit of this country for the construction of an ocean to ocean railway on Canadian territory, Canadian professional, men, engineers and surveyors, as well as Canadian labourers, shall be given the preference in the construction of that work. Is there anything inconsistent in the adoption of that proposition with the introduction later on of the general legislation which the Hon. Minister of Labour proposes to bring down ? The fact that a provision such as my hon. friend from South Waterloo suggests is incorporated in the Bill which we are now discussing will strengthen the hands of the hon. the Minister of Labour in bringing down a measure which will make the law applicable not only to this undertaking but to all undertakings of a similar kind which may come before the parliament of Canada in the future. My hon. friend from South Waterloo has good ground for the introduction of this measure. He has had before him and we have seen upon the statute-books of the great commonwealths to the south of us for years legislation of a similar character. The statesmen to the south of us, whatever may be said of them, have the courage of their convictions when matters affecting the welfare of the working classes of the republic are concerned, and for years past in nearly all states of the union enactments have been on the statute-books providing that the preference shall be given especially on works to which the state or the municipality contributes to citizens of the republic or to those who intend to become citizens of the republic. Let me quote for the information of hon. gentlemen some of the laws which I have found to be in existence on the statute-books of several of the states of the union. I obtained this information from the second special report of the United States Commissioner of Labour. Referring to .New York, at page 771, he says :
In all cases where labourers are employed on public work in this state preference shall be given to citizens of the State of New York.
There is no reason why, when this Bill which makes provision for the construction of a national transcontinental railway is passing its last and final stage as far as this House is concerned, we should not make a similar provision with respect to the work to be done upon it.
Laws of New York, 1902-Vol. 2, page 1099 : * In the construction of public works by the

state or a municipality or by persons contracting with the state or such municipality, only citizens of the United States shall be employed. . . . Each contractor performing work shall keep a list of employees, &c., &c.
Then follows the penalty :
A violation of this section shall constitute a misdemeanour and shall be punishable by a fine of not less than $50 nor more than $500, or imprisonment for not less than thirty days or more than ninety days, or by both.
There is no uncertain sound about that language. There is no doubt as to what it means, and if we were to make a simple provision in the contract we are now dealing with to the effect thait none but Canadians or British subjects shall be employed upon the work, and that any violation of this law shall be punishable in the same way as it is dealt with under the statutes of the state of New York, the time of the House would not be taken up with a discussion as to the best means of enforcing the Alien Labour law respecting matters with which the people generally have to deal. The state of Illinois, another great empire state, makes this provision :
It shall he unlawful for any hoard or commission or any officer or other person, or for any municipality in the state, or any contractor or sub-contractor to employ any person other than native born or naturalized citizens of the United States, or those who have declared their intention of becoming citizens, when such employees are to be paid in whole or part, directly or indirectly, out of any funds raised by taxation. Any treasurer or disbursing officer is personally liable if he knowingly pays alien employees employed on such works.
The state of Pennsylvania makes this provision p. 993 :
None but citizens of the United States shall be employed in any capacity, in the erection, enlargement or improvement of any public building or work within this commonwealth.
Idaho, pp. 229'and 233, makes this provision :
No person not a citizen of the United States, or who has not declared his Intention to become such, or who is not eligible to become such, shall be employed upon any state or municipal work nor shall any such person be employed by any contractor to work on any public works of the state or any municipality.
New Jersey makes this provision :
It shall not be lawful for the state or any municipality within the state, or for any board, committee, commission or other organization having charge of any public work or any construction to employ as a mechanic or labourer thereon, any person who is not a^ the time of such employment a citizen of the United States.
The penalty for the violation of this law is a fine of ?100. The state of California provides that :
No person except a citizen of the United States shall he employed in any department of Mr. CLARKE.
the state, county, city or town government in this state. It shall be unlawful for any person, whether elected, appointed or commissioned to-fill any office in either the state or any municipal government in the state, to appoint or employ any person to perform any duties whatsoever exeept such person be a citizen of the United States.
I might go on and multiply evidence culled from the laws of the several states to prove that the rule on the other side is that citizens of the United States shall be given the preference upon works in which the state or national government or the municipality is interested. I think, in view of the statements which have been presented to this House as to the audacious employment of aliens in the work of surveying this new National Transcontinental Railway, the most effective method that can he adopted is not to wait until the government bring down an alien labour law hut to make a concrete provision in this contract that will prevent the employment of aliens on a work that the people of Canada have to pay for.
I think it was the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who, in his speech this afternoon, expressed sympathy with the remarks which fell from the lips of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk); but then he desired that there should be no embargo or prohibition placed upon the admission of men, eminently skilled in the professions, into this country to assist in the development of any national work or undertaking. There is a special provision in the Alien Labour law at the present time to meet such cases ; but Mr. Speaker, it is little short of an insult to say that we have not in Canada to-day engineers of sufficient capacity, of sufficient experience, of sufficient ability to do any work in engineering or surveying that may be required upon this new road. If the allegations made by the engineering profession in Montreal and Winnipeg are founded upon fact, and if we have these experienced and well qualified professional men in Canada who are aiding in bearing the burdens of this country, it is little short of a shame and a scandal if they are being discriminated against. They are surely entitled to fair-play. In my judgment, and in the judgment, I believe, of a majority of the members of this House, they are entitled, other things being equal, to the preference ; and if the amendment of the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Clare) meets with the approval of the majority of the members of this House, they will get that preference after this contract has been ratified by both branches of the parliament of Canada.
This afternoon reference was made to the action of the government in providing in the Crow's Nest Pass Railway contract that native Canadians should be given the preference upon that work. The construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway was an important work,

but it sinks into insignificance compared witb the gigantic undertaking which the people of Canada are now about to assume. Millions and millions of dollars more are involved in the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway than were involv ed in the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway ; and if it were a commendable act to provide in the Crow's Nest Pass Railway contract that the work should b^ given to Canadian labourers instead of to foreigners, surely we are justified in arguing that the non-appearance of a similar clause in this contract is an evidence either that the government were remiss in their duty to the people of Canada in not inserting a similar provision in this contract, or that the government were in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company refused to allow such a clause to be inserted. Whatever credit the government may have been entitled to for inserting such a clause in the Crow's Nest Pass agreement, they are to be condemned in still greater measure by the people of Canada because, having taken credit for that act of six or seven years ago, they obviously neglected their duty in not insisting on a similar provision in this National Transcontinental Railway contract.
There is another phase of this matter to which I desire to refer very briefly. Sneering and unworthy references have been made to the action of my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) in connection with our Alien Labour law. He has been charged with not being honest and sincere in his advocacy of that measure. He has been charged with being amenable to the party lash in years gone by, because at the request of his leaders he did not press to a division the Alien T.abour Bill which he introduced. But 1 would draw attention to this fact-if I am not stating a fact hon. gentlemen opposite can contradict me-I draw attention to the fact that on every occasion that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), prior to 189(1, introduced his Alien Labour Bill, not one Liberal member who then sat in the House stood up to support him. It surely does not rest in the mouth of the Minister of Labour, who was then in the House, to condemn the member for Leeds, because during all the time the member for Leeds was fighting for the passage of an Alien Labour law the Minister of Labour sat absolutely dumb in his seat. And what can I say of my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell) V He was a colleague of the member for Leeds in this House every ses sion that Bill was being considered. 1 Hansard ' fails to show that on any one occasion the member for York (Mr. Campbell) assisted the member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) in the slightest degree to make that measure law.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: There were very few on your side who supported it.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: That may be quite true: but, at all events, those who were in favour of the Alien Labour law and the principle of protecting Canadian labour were to be found amongst the party which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) supported. Not one single man amongst the Liberals could be found to assist the member for Leeds in the work which he undertook of giving necessary protection to Canadian workmen along our frontier

speechtext: It would be interesting to know why the Bill was not passed.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr Johnston) is not as simple as he looks. The obvious reason why the Bill did not pass is that the member for Leeds could not get sufficient support to pass it. If my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) had been in the House, no doubt he would have broken through party trammels and support- ' ed the hon. member for Leeds.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: He will do so tonight.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I am sure that to-night he will record his vote in favour of the amendment of the hon. member for -South Waterloo. But, Mr. Speaker, public opinion had to be educated in favour of such an Act. I must confess that legislation of the kind is foreign to the statute-books of British colonies ; it was a new departure so far as this parliament was concerned, and it was not until the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) was able to convince, not only the majority in this House, but also the great thinking people of the provinces of Canada that an injustice was being done to Canadian workmen, that he secured sufficient influence to have a measure granting protection to Canadian workmen passed by this parliament, lion, gentlemen opposite take great credit to themselves that the Alien Labour Act became law during the regime of the present government. Whatever credit there is lor the passage of that Act they are certainly entitled to it; but I wish to draw the attention of the House to the fact that in 1896, when the Liberal party came into power, my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) was not deterred ; he persisted in introducing his Bill, and if the Bill did not become law in 1896, it was because of no lack of zeal and no lack of energy on the part of the member for Leeds-it was due to the fact that the right hon. the Prime Minister-asked. my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) to withdraw the Bill for a specific reason. The remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister will be found in 1 Hansard,' second session, 1896. pages 932. 933 and 934. It is unnecessary to quote all that the Prime Minister said, but I extract the following from his remarks :
Therefore, I am disposed to view with some favour the Bill of my hon. friend. But I will claim the privilege of asking him not to pro-

maintopic: S487 COMMONS

speechtext:
ceed further at the present time. The hon. gentleman has stated, what I was not aware of, that correspondence has taken place between the American authorities and the Canadian authorities upon this subject ; and before the hon. gentleman proceeds with this Bill I think it would he advisable for the government to look into this correspondence and see whether it is not possible to avoid such unfriendly legislation. But, if, after taking cognizance of this correspondence, we find there is no way of escaping the conclusion at which my hon. friend has arrived, I will give him every opportunity at the next sitting of the House to press his Bill, if he thinks proper. Therefore I will move the adjournment of the debate.
In the face of that statement of the Prims Minister, I appeal to the hon. member for Oape Breton ; aye, and to the hon. member for West York, is it fair to charge my hon. friend from Leeds with dereliction of duty, when year after year he persisted in bringing this matter before the House? And when in 1896, at the request of the Prime Minister, his Bill stood over until 1897, he had the assurance that if the statements made by him were found to be correct-and they were -the Prime Minister would give him an opportunity in 1897 of introducing and passing the Bill which he had prepared, and which was line for line, and word for word, and letter for letter, as far as applicable. a copy of the Alien Labour law of the United States. Sir, it is only *doing the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) scant justice to say that if Canadian labour has received any protection by the passage of an Alien Labour law. my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) is entitled primarily to the honour-he is entitled to the credit for that legislation, and anything hon. gentlemen opposite may say to the contrary will not deprive him of that credit.
The Alien Labour Act was passed in 1897. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) introduced his Bill in that year, but another bon. member introduced a Bill on the same subject at the same time, and both Bills were referred to a special committee of the House-with what result, Mr. Speaker ? With the result that the Bill of the hon. member for Leeds was shorn of its principal provision, which would have made it a workable measure, and a compromise Bill which came from the hands of the committee was the enactment made. That Bill passed this House without division, and found its way to the Senate. What treatment did it receive there at the hands of the colleagues of those hon. gentlemen who ask the workingmen of the country to give them the credit of taking an interest in organized labour ? When that Bill, which passed this House with practical unanimity, went to the Senate, the leader of the government in the Senate did all that it was possible for him to do to prevent it becoming law. Was that done designedly or by accident ? We have had before us in this House a measure to provide for the Mr. CLARKE.
recognition of the union label. That measure passed this House again and again only to be«killed in the,Senate, and the responsibility for that action was placed on those who constituted the majority of the Senate until last session. A similar attempt was made with regard to the Alien Labour Bill in 1897. It passed this House practically unanimously, but an attempt was made in the Senate to kill it. so as to throw the responsibility for its defeat upon those who constituted the majority in the Senate at that time. Hon. gentlemen opposite would then be able to say : See where the friends of organized labour are ; the majority in the unregenerate, unreformed Senate will not allow this Bill to become law. But now the boot is on the other leg, and it remains to be seen whether the present majority in the Senate will be prepared to pass the Bill recognizing the union label the next time it goes before them. The hon. the Secretary of State, in dealing with the Alien Labour Bill in the Senate in 1897, is reported at page 693 of the Senate Debates to have said :
If we put this on our statute-book, it is an announcement of what our intentions are. Do we propose to follow them up ? I do not think we do.	I notice our Act is
in no way similar to that of the United States. There the officers, such as DeBarry, stationed on the line between Canada and the United States, at Buffalo, Detroit, Ogdensburg, Niagara and several other points, have arbitrary powers and can deport a man without the intervention of a police officer or any judicial authority. We do not propose to lay down any such rule. On the contrary, no action can be taken under this legislation except by the Attorney General for Canada.
On page 694, he is reported to have said further :
What I fear is that by our adopting a law of this kind we will only make matters worse. They will say : ' You adopted a similar law, and it is a justification for us to go on and enforce ours to the extreme letter that we are authorized to do.' That might be the effect of it ; and I do not think it would be really wise to pass this Act. * I do not think it is likely to be enforced, and when it is not enforced it is a pity to place it on tlio statute-book. because it is not on a'line with the views of the people of Canada.
Further on he said :
I advise that it be dropped, because it is not a Bill which should be enforced, unless there was machinery provided, unless we authorized somebody with arbitrary power to act where a man, for instance, crosses from the United States into Canada over the suspension bridge. If we had an officer there who would say : ' You are coming to work in Canada ; we have a law against it, and will force you to go back,' there would be something effective about it. But under this Act persons can come in by the thousands, and it is only when a report is sent

to the Attorney General and he makes inquiry, that any action -would be taken ; and of course the party would by that time be absorbed in the community, and that would be the enl of it. It is something which we do not propose to carry out.
I am sure that my hon. friend from Cape Breton has never read this volume of the 'Senate Debates,' or he would have been shocked at the divergence of opinion which seemed to exist over a matter of such importance amongst hon. gentlemen occupying seats in the same cabinet.
What more need I say in reference to this matter ? I am glad personally to learn that the government has decided to appoint a commission to investigate the causes of complaint respecting the employment of aliens as surveyors and engineers on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Let me emphasize if I can what my hon. friend from South Waterloo so effectively said this afternoon, that the employment of surveyors and engineers who are aliens will practically put Canadian contractors and manufacturers out of court. At any rate, Canadian contractors and manufacturers would feel safer in the hands of competent Canadian engineers of experience, who knew the conditions, than they would feel in the hands of aliens whom they do not know, and who may, for aught we know, be interested in construction companies or companies of other kinds' existing in the United States.
Let me say a word with regard to the appointment of his Honour Judge Winchester. My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) eulogized Mr. O'Donohue, one of the officers of the Labour Department, in his speech this afternoon. I have nothing to say in rebuttal of the high opinion which the hon. member for Winnipeg expressed of Mr. O'Donogliue. I have had the pleasure of the acquaintance of Mr. O'Donoghue for more than thirty years, during which time he has taken an active interest in organized labour in this country. But taking hon. gentlemen opposite at their appreciation of Mr. O'Donoghue, may I ask, is he not the fair-wage officer of the Labour Department ? If so, why was he not sent up to investigate the complaints made by the Canadian engineers and surveyors 1 He is familiar with the work ; he has had experience in inquiring into and reporting upon complaints made from time to time as to violations of the Alien Labour law. Would it not have been fair and reasonable, in view of the multiplicity of these complaints, for the government to have appointed this trained officer of many years' experience, or the Deputy Minister of Labour, Mr. King, who has also had a great deal of experience, to investigate these serious complaints ? But no, they would rather employ an overworked though eminent judge of the County Court of York. The
government would have been entitled to a great deal more credit if they had appointed men of experience, whom the working classes of this country know, and in whom they have confidence in matters of this kind. The government have only appointed a commission to inquire into these serious allegations at the eleventh hour. When the Minister of Labour spoke last, he did not think the matter was as serious as he now thinks it is. He has acted hurriedly in appointing a commission. Why ?. Because, I am safe in saying, the evidence has accumulated to show that the charges which have been made are worthy of serious investigation. Whatever may be the outcome of this investigation or whatever may be the report of the commission, hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are at least entitled to a measure of credit for having forced upon an unwilling department and a derelict government attention to a matter of great importance to the Canadian working people. It is high time, unless this Alien Labour law is to continue a dead letter, that something should be done with it. I have in my hand clippings taken from papers during the past two days giving publicity to several different complaints in respect of this matter-complaints that would be dealt with if we had an efficient labour law or some efficient supervision of aliens coming to this country. The first extract which I shall take the liberty of reading is from the Toronto ' Star.' I am sure the hon. the Minister of Labour will not say, when I quote the ' Star,' that I am quoting from a paper unfriendly to himself personally or to the administration of which he is such a distinguished member. On the 23rd of May, the ' Star ' published an interview with Mr. Basso, on Italian immigration :
Mr. Michael Basso is a well-known citizen of Toronto, of Italian origin, but a British subject. He is a gentleman so highly respected that he acts as court interpreter from time to time in matters involving the interests of his countrymen. Let me say here that we have in Toronto and many other parts of the Dominion thousands of citizens of Italian birth. They are among our best citizens in Toronto and elsewhere. We have no objection to Italians coming into the country, provided their moral and physical condition is unobjectionable, and provided they settle among us, become citizens of Canada, and assist in bearing the burdens which a young country must necessarily bear. But the class of Italians to whom Mr. Basso refers are not that class ; and I take the liberty of drawing the attention of the Minister of Labour to what Mr. Basso says. Mr. Basso is a well known citizen, responsible for anything he says. If he cannot substantiate the statements I am about to read, the public ought to know it. If he can, the minister ought to be indebted to him, and to myself for that matter, for drawing his attention to a condition of things

which does not bode well for the working people and which should be put a stop to at the earliest possible moment:
Italians duped by countrymen.
Michael Basso condemns wholesale navvy importations to Canada. -
Mr. Michael Basso, the well-known Toronto Italian, condemns in strong terms the wholesale importation of Italians to Canada, which has resulted in the flooding o£ Montreal with navvies from Sunny Italy.
'It is a shame how these Italians are brought over and duped by their countrymen,' said Mr. Basso. ' With a few exceptions, the native Italian consuls on this continent are nothing more or less than aiders and abettors of the pernicious padrone system. Those who do not actually connive to induce Italian labourers to come to America wink at the system, which is practically an Italian slave system. It is a disgrace. It is not a nice thing to have to say, but I want to tell the public that the English-speaking Italian consuls on this continent, such as Dr. Harley Smith, the Toronto consul, take more real interest in the Italians than the men who are sent here by the Italian government.
' The majority of those Italians now destitute at Montreal are men who were induced to come here by a man who is connected with a society supported by the Italian government, which is supposed to aid destitute Italians to get back to Italy and to look after them generally here. This man is in the pay of a railway. He gets $5 a day for providing the railroad with navvies, yet he bleeds the workmen and the sub-bosses, too. He advertised last winter that he had work for thousands of workmen, yet I am sure that he did not actually have places for a hundred. Then, when the Italians were brought out from Italy on his representations, the men in charge of the gangs had to pay him from $25 to $75 to procure work for their gangs. This same man, too, charged the individual Italians from $1 to $3 for registering them on his employment register.
' I am afraid that this influx of Italians will create trouble in Toronto next winter. Last winter the city was overcrowded with Italians. The boarding-houses could not accommodate them, and I know of one case where seventeen Italians lived all winter in two rooms. This man has an agent in Toronto, and he is bringing in these new Italians to take places that should be filled by Toronto Italians. The superabundance of Italian labour has already cheapened wages here, and if an extra thousand or two of Italians are left in the city over next winter I do not know what we will do with them.' I
I ask the attention of the hon. Minister of Labour to this statement particularly. It is a statement which okigbt to be investigated at once and its truth or falsity established. In the ' Mail ' of yesterday, there is a despatch from Sault Ste. Marie, dealing with the operation of the Alien Labour law' in that part of Ontario. Might I ask the hon. minister if he has not had his attention drawn to infractions of that law at the Sault ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.

speechtext:
Sault-Ste. Marie, Ont., May 23.-Considerable feeling has been worked up in the Soo ' over the exercise and non-exercise of the Alien Labour laws along the international border. On the American side the officials have been very strict as regards the enforcement of the laws against the Canadian labourers who would go across the river to work, while there has been on this side almost a total neglect of the Canadian law, with the result that many Americans are earning money in Canada and spending it in the United States.
Americans are even employed to a large extent on government works in this vicinity. For instance, two of Hickler Brothers' dredges are just now employed on a contract of widening out the channel above the ship canal, and on the two dredges about sixteen men are at work. Investigation has revealed the fact that out of eight men employed on one of these dredges there is only one solitary resident Canadian. Five of the crew are Americans, and two are said to be British born, but are residing in the United States. On the other dredge three of the crew are American citizens. There are a good many men in the Canadian ' Soo ' who have been out of employment for some time, who are capable of filling, and who would be glad to have, the places of the Americans who should now find it easy to get other work at home, since the immigration officers across the line are sending home all the Canadians they can find.
Every morning and evening a number of boats cross the river between the veneer mill on this side and Neasville, a suburb of the Michigan ' Soo,' carrying Americans who work at the mill to and from their homes across the river. There are said to be several other flagrant violations of the law continually going on.
The people of this town would not feel so keenly over the matter were it not for the manner in which the American officers are enforcing the laws of their country, after which the Canadian laws were framed as a measure of protection. So long as the Canadian people were allowed to work across the river, there was no great objection (o allowing the much more numerous army of American workmen to come here. But now that the United States refuses to allow Canadians to earn a living in the American * Soo,' it is held that it is absolutely necessary that the labour market here be kept for the people of the town, and not those of a foreign country.
I am sure we all agree In the closing sentiment of this article. If our people are not

permitted to obtain employment on tlie American side, they certainly should be given tha preference on their own side. If they are displaced on the American side and their places taken by citizens of the United States, when they return to Canada they shohild not find themselves displaced at home also by Americans. The last report I shall read is from the Ottawa 1 Citizen.' X could read dozens of statements made in newspapers published in almost every part of the country complaining of this condition of things, but 1 shall rest my case on what I have just read and what I am about to read from the Otttawa ' Citizen ' :
Deported to Canada.
Ogdensburg, N.Y., May 24.-Eleven persons, former residents of lower Canada, have been arrested by United States Immigration Inspector Farrell and deported to Canada. They had all become public charges.
If we are to have an Alien Dab our law, we ought to enforce it ; we ought to make provision that it can be enforced ; we ought to make it easy of enforcement ; we ought to make it of speedy enforcement ; we ought to make it inexpensive to enforce. If we do not, it will be absolutely a dead letter, for the reasons given by the Secretary of State when he asked the Senate, in 1897, to throw out the Bill. If Canadian workmen feel aggrieved, if Canadian workmen feel that their places have been unfairly taken by Americans, unless they have immediate recourse to the police court, where having made affidavit to the facts they can have a summons issued and the offender brought before the court, the Act cannot be enforced. No matter how earnest, no matter how zealous, the Minister of Labour and his officials may be he will find the Act, in his hands, a dead letter. There can be no doubt, I repeat, of the effect of the law if the amendment which the hon. member for South Waterloo has presented is adopted by this 'House. In the construction of this great National Transcontinental Railway, involving an expenditure of from $100,000,000 to $150,000,000, provision will be made that our own people shall get the first opportunity of employment ; that, so far as the professional work is concerned, surveying and engineering, it shall be done by Canadians and not by aliens and foreigners. Imagine, if you can, Mr. Speaker, any state in the union pledging its credit to the extent of $100,000,000 or $150,000,000 for the construction of a public work, and Canadian engineers and surveyors being brought over there to displace American professional men. How long would the people of any state, or all the states, tolerate such a condition of affairs ? Not for one minute. But if the suggestion of my hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) becomes law, in this great national undertaking, involving such an immense expenditure raised upon the public credit, Canadian professional men
and Canadian labouring men will have the first opportunity of employment-and they are entitled to it, they should have it. But, if it is found-and this shows the great care and wisdom with which this resolution has been drawn by my hon. friend from South Waterloo-that sufficient labour of Canadian or British origin cannot be had to expedite the work, then, upon the certificate of the Minister of Labour that such workmen cannot be found, the provision for the employment of Canadian and British workmen shall be relaxed so that outsiders may be employed and the work proceed as expeditiously as the most ardent promoter of the enterprise could desire. I hope the Minister of Labour will withdraw his objections to the amendment. It will strengthen his hands in this House and strengthen his position before the people of this country if he allows this provision to be incorporated in the contract. It will be an evidence that hon. gentlemen opposite intend that this shall be a truly national work. Would it not be a disgraceful thing to be said in years to come that this road was constructed, that this great national highway from ocean to ocean every foot on Canadian soil, was surveyed and engineered by foreigners and constructed by alien labour ? If the amendment of the hon. member for South Waterloo prevails, it will be impossible to make that statement. We have competent engineers in Canada, and we have hundreds and thousands of able bodied workmen, and our solicitude and our care should be that these men should be given the first consideration, and only after they are fully employed should aliens be given an opportunity to work upon an undertaking the money for which is being provided upon the credit and at the expense of the people of Canada.

goes further. In order to justify the position taken by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) he refers to the legislation adopted in the United States. My hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) need have no anxiety about that. The law will be made sufficiently ample and. fdll ,!to meet requirements of this kind. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) spoke of complaints about the treatment meted out to Canadians with respect to this enterprise. Our answer is that provision has been made and is being made now to investigate these complaints,
and if they are found to be justified and accurate such steps will be taken as will justify the conduct of the government since 1S97. The conduct of the government has been actuated by the principle that organized labour throughout the country is to bo protected within the limits of what is right. There is not one class only to be protected in this country. I am speaking for myself. I want to do what is right for organized labour, but when I want to do what is right for organized labour, I want to respect vested interests and the rights of corporations and capitalists. It is our settled policy that so far as all enterprises carried on with the aid of public money in this country are concerned, there should be ample provision made by legislation of a general character, to protect the labourer and to give him that to which he is fairly entitled, the advantage of a preference under equal conditions. That is what the Canadian labourer is entitled to and what he should receive. We should so frame our legislation-and it should be introduced almost immediately and before this Bill has been sanctioned-that it should have for effect to protect the Canadian labourer within the limits of what is right, so that he should have the benefit of any expenditure that is being made in this country, and that he should have the preference. Not only should that apply to the Canadian 'labourer ; it should apply also to the professional men, so that all expenditure connected either with engineering or with labour, should be so made that Canadians should have first choice and Canadians should have the advantage. That is the settled policy of the government; it has been settled for some time and in so far as this country is concerned, that policy will be placed on the statute-book before this Bill becomes law.
