speechtext:
I think that the Minister of Justice must have been hit pretty hard by the remarks of the hon member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) ; otherwise we would not .have seen this petty display of temper. A measure designed to overcome the present injustice is to be brought down by the government and it has been in the contemplation of the government for some time. That is the statement of the government through the hon. Minister of Justice. It is a remarkable thing, if this has been in the contemplation of the government so long, that not one word with regard to so important a subject was said in the speech from the Throne, and not one word has been heard with regard to it until within the past week or ten days when the matter was brought up from this side of the House. The Minister of Labour has told the House and the country that all he has done after these complaints have been pouring in upon him for weeks, is to write certain letters to the officers -of this company. After all that has occurred;

after complaints of this kind have been heard from all over the country for months, then, for the first time, we learn from the government that they have had this general legislation in contemplation for a long time. It is a pity that they had not taken parliament and the country into their confidence in the speech from the Throne, because an important matter of that kind was more worthy of mention in that speech than many of the trivial subjects mentioned in it. As a matter of fact we have every reason to believe that the government have not had this matter in contemplation. We accept the words of the Minister of Justice that the government have had this in contemplation for some time, but we are entitled to give our own interpretation to the words ' some time ' and we do not give these words that extended meaning which the language of the Minister of Justice might be interpreted to attach to them. My hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) says that the member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) shall not escape him. Well, I have not observed any particular disposition on the part of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) to escape the Minister of Justice or any one else in this House. Has the Minister of Justice observed any intense desire on the part of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) to escape him ? I have not observed it, and I do not know thaj; any one except the. Minister of Justice has observed that desire on the part of the hon. member (Mr. Clarke) at any time. He wishes to know why special treatment should be meted out to this particular company. Might I answer the question by asking another question of the Minister of Justice ? Why was it that special treatment was meted out to the company that built the Crow's Nest Pass Railway ? In the contract which has been laid before the House, provisions to all intents and purposes the same as those proposed by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) were inserted and were made binding on the company that were building the Crow's Nest Pass Railway. If this was a good subject for a general law, why was not the course now proposed to be adopted, carried out in that case ? Why was not a general law framed in that instance ? Why was that company singled out for what the Minister of Justice considers invidious treatment in regard to this important question ?
We would be very glad to have this general legislation passed. When it is placed before the House, it will meet with our support if it is designed in proper language to remedy the great grievance which is now being complained of. Ret me say. however, that in the meantime while this investigation is going on and while this general legislation is being framed by the hon. Minister of Justice and is being passed by parliament we should not forget that j -the surveys on this road are being made by I Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
engineers from the United States, and that Canadian engineers capable of performing that work are going without that employment to which they are entitled out of the moneys voted by this parliament for the purposes of the government. This is not the first occasion upon which we have heard of amendments to the general law resulting from discussions we have had. We have had suggestions from the hon. Minister of Justice with regard to more than onei subject. All that I have to say is that if the opposition have succeeded by the arguments which they have addressed to the House in inducing the government to make these changes in the general law, I think they are entitled to the gratitude of the country and especially to that of those Canadians, whether engineers, or1 whether labouring men, or whether belonging to other occupations who during the past five or six or seven months have been excluded from working upon this railway and have seen that work performed by men from the other side of the line. I did not intend to take part in the discussion upon this subject but I thought it only right.in view of what the hon. Minister of Justice has said to make these few remarks and to point out to him as I have done that we need not go to the United States of America as he has asked my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) to go in order to find safeguards of this kind, because, as I have already said, he has only to look back to the contract respecting the Crow's Nest Pass Railway to find that exactly the same provisions were made, not in regard to all companies in the country, but in regard to the company then performing a public work, which certainly was of very minor importance to that which is now proposed to be undertaken by the people of Canada.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say one word in regard to the argument which is advanced in this House as a defence for voting down this proposed amendment. It is an argument which has been addressed to this House ou more than one occasion during the present session. When we have a special Bill before us and when we desire to put into that Bill some special provisions to provide for something that ought to be provided for there and no where else, we are told that it requires to be put in a general Act, that this should be allowed to pass and that a general Act would contain a provision for it. V,'lien the amendment was moved to control freight rates in connection with this road we were treated with a similar argument to the effect that such a provision should go into the Railway Act and not into this special Act. Now then when we desire to make a special provision to protect the labouring interests of Canada we are told that it ought to go into a general Act and not be put into this special Act.

It is the special Act that we have before us now and it is for us to deal with one thing at a time. This is a great and important public work for which the people of Canada are paying and paying almost absolutely, and therefore it is most proper that a special provision should be placed in this Act instead of a general Act being introduced for that purpose. But suppose we were willing to take the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) at his word, in view of the history of the past, what confidence would we have that he would be likely to introduce a Bill that would answer the requirements ? We were *told exactly the same thing when my hon. friend from South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) introduced his Alien Labour Law. The government said that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) would introduce a Bill that would have a general application to all parts of the country. He did introduce that Bill. Of whati use is that Bill to-day ? I have a report from a paper in British Col-unmbia, regarding a prosecution under that law, and what is the report from that province ? The Bill is practically worthless. What reason have we for believing that the general Bill to be introduced by the government would not be equally worthless some months hence ? Why should not we have a special provision in connection with this great undertaking ? This is a special Transcontinental Railway for which the country is paying and it is in connection with this undertaking alone that we should deal with the question at the present time. Afterwards, if the government desire to go further and introduce a general law, I have no doubt whatever but that it will receive* the support of hon. members on this side of the House provided it commends itself to their judgment as a useful measure. But if the government introduce a law similar to that which they introduced before for the purpose of deluding and misleading the labouring class of this country they are not likely to get the support of hon. members on this side of the House. I remember very distinctly that the defects and weaknesses of that law were pointed out and that it was positively and emphatically declared that none of the evils were likely to occur that we said from this side of the House would occur. What has been the experience since that law was adopted? The law is worthless to-day. If any one attempts to carry on a prosecution under it what is the result ? He has to ask the permission of a judge or a police magistrate and if there is no police magistrate in the district, he has to get the authority of die Minister of Justice or the Solicitor General and these officers may not give him the necessary authority. How many prosecutions have taken place under the law ? When an attempt is made to prosecute, it is found, as in British Columbia at the present time,
that the law is of no value whatever that they cannot prosecute under it with any hope of securing a conviction and that they cannot turn aliens back from the country who have come here in open violation of the law.
Mr. RALjtrf SMITH (Vancouver). Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I had not the opportunity of being present at the debate this afternoon, and I did not hear any of the speeches on this question excepting the speech of the hon. senior member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The subject of the debate on the third reading of the Bill is similar to the subject that was discussed in committee. I just desire to occupy the time of the House for about a minute and to say that I cannot believe that there is any sincerity in any proposition that will place a I'estriction upon the operation of a single company in this country, especially as the question with which it deals affects the whole country. As I said before, when discussing this matter the question is one that calls for general legislation. What does it matter to the workingmen of this country that the Grand Trunk Railway are restricted as to the employment of certain labourers, while the Canadian Pacific Railway are employing certain labourers, while the whole of the coal mines are employing alien labourers and while the manufacturers who are subsidized by a protective tariff are employing alien labourers ? What does it matter to the workingmen of this country if all the industries are to be permitted to employ those whom they like and one industry is singled out and restricted 1 I desire to say that I do not think any hon. member in this House will question my sincerity

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.

Any more than I question the sincerity of my hon. friend from West Toronto. I believe that my hon. friend from West Toronto is quite sincere in desiring to do something in the interests of the working men. I do not care very much whether the members of the opposition believe that I am sincere in that interest or whether they do not. All I have to say is that I feel sincere and I do not think tne workingmen of this country would consider favourably for one minute the proposal that has been presented to this House and which discriminates not at all in their own interests. The men working for different factories and different railways want to know where they come in. What does it matter to them if the industries that employ them are not to be restricted the same as the industry which is referred to in the amendment ? General legislation is the real remedy and I want to say that I shall vote against that amendment.
I will do that for the reason that the Minister of Labour, some weeks ago dis-

cussed this whole matter with me ; I expressed my anxiety for legislation of this kind, and he promised to introduce it, and of course I believe the Minister of Labour is sincere, while lion, gentlemen opposite do not seem to think so. In the debate to-night, there have been insinuations against the operation of the labour bureau, and insinuations against the efficiency of the Alien Labour law. Let me point out that in 1888 the United States passed an Alien Labour law, and although the Conservatives were in power many years after that, they never passed a similar Act. As to the labour bureau, it is well known that for many years there was an agitation in this country for the establishment* of a labour bureau, but the Conservative party then in power never brought such a bureau into existence, although it is true that prior to one general election they promised a commission. In view of the history of both political parties in reference to labour legislation, and when we find the Conservatives at this particular time supporting an amendment of this kind against one particular industry, I believe that we have every reason for questioning their sincerity. The Minister of Labour has promised that he will bring in a law that will apply to all industries. That is the right kind of legislation; that is the legislation I will support. I will oppose the amendment because I believe the government will bring in general legislation which will prove a remedy for the whole of this grievance. _

speechtext: In view of the experience of the past, is not the hon. member (Mr. Ralph Smith) a little chary in taking the word of the government that they will introduce a general law which will be effective ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
There is a very painful phase of this whole matter, and that is, that no matter how good a proposal may be, if it comes from a member of the opposition, it is opposed and voted down by the supporters of the government. We have now before us an amendment Mr. RALPH SMITH.
brought in by a member of the opposition, and it is opposed by the government and its supporters, who have not given a single good reason why they should vote against it. First, we had the Minister of Labour, and he opposed this amendment because, as he said, he would bring in a similar measure, wider in its scope. He does not for a moment say that the amendment is not for the benefit of the country, but he asked his followers to vote against it, simply because he promises to bring in a general measure at some future day. Well, we have such a general measure now on the statute-book, and the labour people of the country know how extremely ineffective it is. Here we have a great corporation receiving greater privileges from the government than were ever before accorded, and is this not the time and place to pass special legislation to protect the Canadian workingmen who have to pay the taxes to build this railway ? We have complaints which are undoubtedly well founded that at the present time this Grand Trunk.Pacific Company is violating the existing Alien Labour law, and does it not appeal to the common sense of the House that such violation should be put an end to at once ? Then we have the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) opposing the amendment. He did not oppose it because it was unwise, but because forsooth it does not exclude British subjects as well as aliens. Whenever any proposal is made in this parliament to further solidity and cement the ties that bind the various portions of this great empire, it acts on the member for La-belle like a red rag on a bull, and he at once rises to oppose such a measure. Then we have the member for Burrard (Mr. Mac-pherson) who thinks the amendment is wise and salutory, but he announced he would vote against it because the government he supports was the first to put a tax of $500 upon Chinese. Next, the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell), opposed the amendment, and his only reason was that the government introduced an Alien Labour law, and which we all know has proved inadequate to exclude contract labour from the United States. Then we have the Minister of Justice announcing that he will oppose the amendment and his opposition is apparently based upon the grounds, that the member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) introduced an Alien Labour law just previous to an election. Not one of these gentlemen opposite has ventured to give a common sense reason why he will vote against this amendment. As I have said, we have this great corporation receiving immense privileges from the country, and yet it is undoubtedly true that they are at present employing in the surveys of this route a very large number of foreigners. I have in my hand a circular, presumably authentic, from the Amalgamated Society of Canadian Engineers who allege that the work now being done in Manitoba-a part of the country in which

the engineering difficulties should not be great-is extremely expensive to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
It is natural that it should be so. The engineers employed being strangers to the topography of the country, it is quite natural that they should commit blunders which Canadian engineers more conversant with the topography of the country would not make. Is this not a deplorable condition of affairs that ought to enlist the sympathy of the government ? I am glad to hear that an investigation is to take place; but why was not Mr. O'Donoghue sent to investigate this matter as soon as the complaint was made, nearly a year ago ? We spend hundreds of thousands of dollars every year in bonusing industries-what for ? To provide employment for Canadians. Yet here is an opportunity by which we can provide for the employment of Canadians without the expenditure of a single dollar. These American engiueeers who are carrying on these surveys will no doubt endeavour as far as possible to bring their friends in to work for them instead of employing Canadians in their parties. But further than that we all know that engineers engaged in surveying in the country have great opportunities of knowing where profitable contracts can be got. They have opportunities to give tips to manufacturers and.contractors which no other class of men have. Is it not natural to suppose that these men. if Americans, will give that information to their friends on the other side of the line instead of to Canadians ? What an advantage it would be to this country to have Canadians occupying these positions instead of Americans, for this reason alone ? And what a disgrace it would be in future years if it could be said that this great Transcontinental Railway, which was to be a national undertaking- that was one of the chief arguments in its favour at the beginning-had been engineered entirely by foreigners ? Is it possible that we have not in Canada engineers capable of surveying and building a line of railway such as this ? Has Canada not given to the world dhiring the last thirty years more eminent engineers than any other country in the world in proportion to its population ? Have we not as good schools for turning out engineers as are to be found on the continent ? I believe the School of Practical Science in Toronto and the School of Science in connection with McGill University are equal to any others on the continent. and they have turned out engineers who are filling the highest positions not only on this continent, but in Europe. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is quite satisfied that his countryman, that eminent engineer, Sir Percy Girouard, should find employment under the British flag; he is quite satisfied, no doubt, that hundreds of millions of capital to build this raiway shall come from British hands; but at the same 111
time he wishes to prevent British subjects from other parts of the empire from coming in here, and would treat them exactly as he would foreigners. In view of the fact that we have engineers who are the equal of any in the world, I think it would be in every way to the financial advantage of the country that we should employ Canadian engineers on the proposed railway. Is it not the duty of the government of the day to take advantage of this opportunity, and not wait until a better general law is passed, which may be a year from now ? because we have not had any notice of it until this evening.
I propose to vote for the amendment, not because it is moved by the hon. member for South Waterloo, who sits on this side of the House, Mut because I believe that this House should take every opportunity it can to throw trade and work into the hands of Canadians. Here is an opportunity that will cost the country nothing. We are doing many things that cost us hundreds of thousands and millions of dollars, to throw work into the hands of Canadian people. Here is an opportunity to throw work into the hands that will cost the country nothing. Why, then, should we not be Canadians in this matter ? Not a word has been said by any hon. gentleman opposite in contradiction of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for South Waterloo ; but hon. gentlemen opposite will' vote against the amendment because it emanates from a member of the opposition. I trust that this spirit will not always prevail. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Ralph Smith), who poses as the sincere friend of- labour in this country, intends to vote against the amendment, because he says, forsooth, that he thinks it is insincere. Is that an argument that will influence any one who is open to conviction ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to say that I never gjfve that as a reason. My reason was because it did not apply to all the industries of this country.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will no doubt have an opportunity later on, if the government bring in a genera! measure, to vote for that measure ; but in the meantime here is a measure that applies at once, and that we know will be effective. I have no sympathy for those men who pose as the friends of labour, but who, when an opportunity presents itself, find some flimsy excuse for failing to support a measure in the interest of labour. Because his party, or that party which he always votes with, opposes this amendment, the hon. gentleman forsooth cannot find it in his heart to vote for it. Mr. Speaker, I trust that a different spirit will prevail, and that when an amendment is proposed in this House, there will be some men independent enough, whether they call themselves independent



or not, to vote for it on its merits, and not simply because it emanates from one party or the other.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this discussion this evening, but some of the observations made by hon. gentlemen opposite are sufficiently interesting to cause members on this side of the House to make some remarks. I desire to say at the outset that it is interesting to have from members on the Conservative side of the House the admission which we have had tonight, namely, that during the eighteen years that the Conservative party were in power, they absolutely refused to do anything whatever to benefit the workingmen of this country. I want to call the attention of workingmen throughout the entire length and breadth of this country to the admission made by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) this, evening, that notwithstanding that his party were in power here for many years, yet they refused year after year to do anything for the benefit of the workingmen of Canada. It is all very well for my hon. friend to come forward here and say that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) was doing his whole duty.
In my judgment, the hon. member for Leeds was not doing his entire duty. On divers occasions he had introduced alien labour legislation, but had he been sincere he would have pressed his Bills to a conclusion, and thus ascertained who are the friends and who are the enemies of alien labour legislation. Not having done this, he did not, in my judgment, do his whole duty. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) went further. He said that in 1896, after the present government came to power, the hon. member for Leeds still persisted in introducing his Alien Labour Bill, and my hon. friend then proceeded to enlighten the House regarding what transpired in the Senate. He would have this House believe that the Liberal party in the upper chamber were opposed to labour legislation. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that if the Senate were desirous of passing such legislation in the year 1897, there was nothing to prevent their doing so. When they found it advisable to throw out government measures in the Senate, they did so in 1897 and in some subsequent years. The hon. member for West Toronto need not hug the delusion that the people are not familiar with the record of the Conservative party on this subject. The working people in this country know very well that year after year before 1896, when hon. gentlemen opposite held office, these people, who are now so anxious to show their sympathy with labour, did nothing. Yet to-night we have them proclaiming that they are the true friends of labour. The hon. member for West Toronto expressed the hope that when the time came for a vot * Mr. E. D. SMITH.
on this particular amendment, I would be found supporting it. Mr. Speaker, I shall not be found supporting it; and if I do not, it is because it is not such an amendment as the workingmen desire us to pass ; but I may here say that when legislation is introduced in this House that is really in the interests of the workingman, that is intended to meet the requirements of the workingmen, that will apply, not only to one corporation, but to every corporation of this country, I will be found supporting that legislation. That is the legislation which, to my mind, is required by the workingmen of this country, and which, I trust, will be introduced and pressed to a conclusion by this government.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Why did the hon. gentlemen not support the resolution of the hon. member for South Waterloo In 1901, if he is always ready to support legislation in the interests of the workingmen ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
I propose to give ample justification for any vote I have given upon this question ; and I tell my hon. friend that if it be shown that the Alien Labour law is defective, I am here to ask the government to bring forward, at the earliest possible moment, legislation which will be effective and meet the requirements of the case. It is important that the workingmen should know the position occupied by the Conservative party on this particular question. That is the point I desire brought home to the people, and upon which the working people are being educated. Long ago they reached the conclusion that if they have any friends, it is not in the Conservative party they will be found. The hon. member for West Toronto speaks a great deal about the union label legislation introduced last year. I want to ask him to real from the Montreal ' Gazette.' That paper is the leading organ of the Conservative party in the jirovince of Quebec, and is also the organ of hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. gentleman has not treated this House to any extracts from that Conservative organ. Let him take up the files of the ' Gazette ' and ' Industrial Canada,' the organ of the manufacturers, and find out what they have to say about this question. He will do so no doubt at a future date. I suppose he has carefully collated all these extracts, both from the Montreal ' Gazette ' and ' Industrial Canada,' and at a later date will read them to this House. The workingmen of this country know well that before 1890 there was very little security for them on government contracts. I desire to call the attention of this House to the fact that since 1897 provision has been made by this government that railway contractors and all contractors receiving government aid shall be obliged, first arid foremost, to pay the wages if the men. That was not the case before 1890. Did it ever occur to the Conservative party, during their long term of eighteen

years in power, that the workingmen of Canada did not deserve treatment of this kind ? Not at all. It never dawned on them for one moment. A contractor could go and get his money and subsidies whenever he wanted them, and no question was asked. He was not asked whether he paid his workingmen or not, and it is notorious that in many instances. before 1896 the contractors left this country and left their labourers unpaid. This government very wisely provided that these things shall not occur hereafter. These are some of the things that, in my judgment, will condemn the opposition. The hon. member for West Toronto was deeply interested on behalf of the Canadian manufacturers. He fairly wept over the fate that would overtake the Canadian manufacturers as the result of the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific. I want him to take that contract and compare it with the contract which the government he supported entered into with the Canadian Pacific Railway for the construction of that railway, and then let him point out whether the contract we are considering to-night provides better terms for the Canadian manufacturers than the contract his friends entered into with the Canadian Pacific Railway. What stock did the Canadian Pacific Railway or the government of that day take in the Canadian manufacturers ? We have provided that the manufacturers shall be looked after. The contract we are considering takes notice of them. The contract that we are discussing here to-night provide i that the Canadian manufacturer shall be recognized.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Why should it not provide that Canadian labour should be recognized ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: The contract provides that in the construction of this railway, recognition is to be given to all industries of Canada, the labour industry included. Therefore, it is that I desire that the labourers of this country should know that better treatment is assured them as a result of this contract than was ever assured by a contract entered into by a Conservative government. I wish to point out that the Canadian manufacturer receives better treatment than he ever received at the hands of a Conservative administration. It is for these reasons that the contract that we are considering commends itself to the judgment of every class in this country.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? If this contract commends itself to the judgment of Canadian workmen, why are they applying to the Canadian government to prevent the employment of alien labourers on this great work, to the detriment of Canadians ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
The Canadian workmen have not applied to this goveru-1114
ment' or to any other authority for such legislation as has been proposed by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare). And I want to say, further, that if the hon. gentleman submits that legislation to any body of organized labour in this country he will be told that that is not the legislation that the workmen of Canada demand.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Have not the Society of Civil Engineers requested the government to deport the Americans who are now engaged on this work, and who outnumber Canadians on the work two to one ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I am not going to permit my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) to get away from the question I am discussing and the question which he himself asked and I answered. The hon. gentleman will not rise in his place and say that any body of organized labour, engineers or others, came before any authority in this country and asked for legislation on the lines of the resolution proposed by the hon. member for South Waterloo.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Alex. Johnston) says that no body of engineers has made such representation. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if it is not true that a memorial has been sent by the Society of Engineers to every member of this House ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: If memorials have been sent, they have not asked for legislation dealing with a particular corporation. The men interested in labour legislation in this country are not behind this amendment. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) had his opportunity to promote legislation beneficial to the working classes of this country. For eighteen years his friends were in power. And what is the record of the hon. gentleman during that time ? Did he ever rise in his place to support the proposals of his desk-mate the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) ? There was a time when the hon. gentleman was a great man in the councils of his party previous to 1890. Did he ever demand from the party of which he was a faithful follower that justice should be done to the workingmen of Canada ? It is not in the records. But when his desk-mate stood up and pretended to be doing something in the interest of the workingmen, my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) gently pulled his coat tail to get him to sit down again.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston, Cape Breton) is misrepresenting me, whether ignorantly or deliberately I do not know, but he is doing it all the same.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule! to say that he was supporting the legislation introduced at different times previous to 1S96 by the hon. member for South Leeds ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. gentleman understands. It would be a very difficult thing for me to judge.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: But, fortunately for us, we have the record of what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) was thinking about. And that record shows that for eighteen years the hon. gentleman never rose and proposed legislation that would benefit the workingmen of this country.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I tell the hon. gentleman distinctly and deliberately that the record does not show anything of the kind, and I say now, and say it advisedly, in the face of the statement I have made, that the hon. gentleman is deliberately misrepresenting me.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Then I understand that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) was supporting the legislation introduced by my hon. friend from South Leeds (Mr. Taylor). Are we to understand that ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I am not responsible for what the hon. gentleman understands.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: It would be interesting for the members of this House and for the people of this country to have a statement from the hon. gentleman to-night as to whether he was supporting the legislation introduced by the hon. member for South Leeds previous to 1896 or not. It is true I have not examined the records very carefully. It may be that ' Hansard ' will reveal that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) stood up and made several long speeches, as was his wont, supporting this measure. If the hon. gentleman will say that that is the case, if he will point out to us that he ever stood up and, in the face of his party leaders, pressed this legislation to a division, I will take back all that I have said on this phase of the question. But, if he cannot show that he has done that, I think I have a perfect right, and the people have a perfect right, to conclude that my hon. friend from East Grey, notwithstanding his protestations, was not sympathetically disposed toward the legislation of the hon. member for South Leeds. All I have to say about this question is that, in my judgment, the present government, which has held power since 1896 has done something to recognize the rights of labour in Canada. It may well be that much remains to be done. But, so far as I am concerned, I am satisfied that the government will in the future, as it has in the past, see to it that proper provision is made with regard to the labourers of this country, and that the protection which is rightly theirs will be given them.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
I think that the answer of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston) only shows his insincerity. Last session I had the honour of introducing a motion in this House to the effect that all supplies should be purchased in Canada that might be required to construct equip and operate, &c. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston) then supported that motion. He supported it on the ground that it would be a protection to our Canadian manufacturers and incidentally to Canadian labourers and Canadian mechanics. That motion was voted down. The hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) was opposed to it and nearly every other gentleman who has risen to-night to speak against the amendment of the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Clare) opposed it, but when the agreement came down we found that notwithstanding the fact that these gentlemen had voted against it almost identically the same clause had been put in the contract. Then all these gentlemen raised their voices in praise of this clause which had been put in the contract to protect Canadian manufacturers and Canadian labourers although they had voted it down when the motion emanated from this side of the House. If the hon. gentleman was consistent then when an opportunity was given him to-night to do something to protect Canadian engineers, Canadian labourers, Canadian workmen, he should take the same course that he took last year in regard to the Canadian manufacturer, and should

have supported the amendment moved by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare). I was not surprised at the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) voting against the manufacturers last year because his course in this House has always been inconsistent in regard to the manufacturing industries of this country. We find him going down to Montreal and making protectionist speeches ; then he comes back into the House and always votes against anything in favour of protection when it emanates from the opposition. As far as I am concerned I see no reason why this amendment should not pass and become part of this Bill. The amendment introduced last year was on exactly the same principle. It was voted down by hon. gentlemen supporting the government with the exception of the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) and one or two others but was afterwards adopted by the government and placed in the Bill. The amendment which is now introduced by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Sir. Clare) is exactly on the same principle. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Sir. Johnston) says that no organized body has asked that this amendment should be moved or that legislation of this sort should be asked. 1 care not whether they have asked or not, we are here to safeguard the interests of our Canadian people and it is our duty to be on the alert and see that provisions are put into this Bill which will amply safeguard our people. But I say they have asked. There is not a"'member in this House who does not know that the engineers in this country have represented to them through circulars which have been sent to every member that to-day American engineers are being employed in all the important positions in connection with the surveys that are now going on and I say that now Is the time to act; before this Bill passes away from us, before we finally vote on it we should introduce an amendment, and When this Bill becomes law it will become effective, and then a preference will be given not to the Americans but to our own British subjects.

speechtext:
I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Jabel Robinson :
That the Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend the same by adding thereto the following section as section No.	:-
(1)	It shall be lawful for the government at any time hereafter upon six months' notice to the Pacific Company to expropriate, acquire and take over the whole undertaking, railways, branch lines, terminals, appurtenances, rolling stock, equipment, hereditaments and real and personal property of the Pacific Company, including the unexpired term of the lease of the eastern division, but not including moneys, securities for moneys and choses in action, and to own and operate the said railways and branch lines and other property.
(2)	Immediately upon the expiration of six months from the date of service of such notice upon the Pacific Company the government may enter into possession of, and the Pacific Company shall deliver to the government possession of the said railways, branch lines, terminals, appurtenances, rolling stock, equipment, hereditaments and real personal property.
(3)	If in such case the government and the Pacific Company shall fail to agree upon the amount of compensation to be paid to the Pacific Company for the property so expropriated, acquired and taken over by the government, the same shall be determined by arbitrators to be appointed in the manner provided in the 47th clause of the original agreement. *
(4)	The arbitrators in considering, arriving at and making their award, shall have regard to and take into account the following matters :[DOT]-[DOT]
(a.) No allowance shall be made or sum awarded for, or on the basis of past or future profits or earning powers, or by wTay of good will or upon any speculative basis or for disappointment or by reason of the sale being compulsory, and the gross amount to be allowed or credited to the Pacific Company before taking into account deductions and sums of money to be retained, shall not in any case exceed the actual value of the property taken over, having Mr- PRINGLE.
regard to and on the basis of the matters immediately hereinbefore provided for.
(b.) Account shall be taken of the total amount of all payments, outlays and contributions by the government whether as money, land, interest paid without recourse, or otherwise on account or in connection with the property taken over and the gross sum otherwise payable by the government shall in addition to any other deduction to be made, be reduced in the proportion which this sum bears to the total cost of the property taken over. Such total cost shall be based upon and shall include the original cost of construction as defined in the scheduled agreements, together with any subsequent expenditure (not being working expenditure) upon capital account for betterments.
(c.) The arbitrators shall take an account of all bonds, mortgages and debts constituting a charge upon the property taken over, and also of the amount of the liability of the government for the Pacific Company by guarantee or otherwise, and the government shall thereupon be taken to have assumed direct liability as between the government and the Pacific Company for the payment of all these debts, charges and liabilities, and to have undertaken to indemnify the Pacific Company from liability or action, and this being done the total amount of these debts, charges and liabilities so ascertained shall by the a ward be set off against or deducted from the sum of money otherwise payable to the Pacific Company, and the balance shall be awarded to be paid by the government to the Pacific Company, or by the Company to the government as the case may be, with interest at per cent from the. date of taking possession.
(5)	The government shall not exercise the said power of expropriating and acquiring the said undertaking, railways, branch lines and other property of the Pacific Company unless and until parliament shall have first made provision by an Act or Acts to be passed in that behalf, for authorizing the raising and payment of the compensation to be awarded by the arbitrators as aforesaid.
(6)	In case the tenth parliament of Canada shall at its first session make such provision, and in case the said power of expropriation shall be exercised within one year after the prorogation of the first session of the said tenth parliament, the gross sum to be allowed or credited to the Pacific Company as compensation as hereinbefore provided, shall not exceed the actual cost to the Pacific Company of the property expropriated, acquired or taken over by the government, and an addition of ten per centum of such portion thereof as shall be actually payable to the Pacific Company after deductions and set off as hereinbefore mentioned.
I propose to say something with regard to this important amendment; an amendment which, in fact, goes to the substance of the whole transaction, which has occupied the attention of parliament now for such a long time. I may explain that, knowing, as I did, that the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) intended to introduce an amendment along the same lines, I asked the hon. gentleman to second this amendment, and his name appears upon the paper which I have just forwarded to you. Mr. Speaker. The right of expropriation -is regarded as an extraordinary remedy; to some extent as a power to be exercised only in

exceptional cases. But we are now dealing with an extraordinary state of things, as I think has become very evident during this debate. It is a measure that is to be resorted to, of course, only where the interest of the public demands that such a course should be taken. I believe that the interests of the country are sufficiently at stake here to warrant parliament in determining that such a remedy should be open to the people of Canada at a future date, and perhaps at a very early date, as indicated by the last clause of this amendment ; a clause which has direct reference to an appeal to the people for their verdict upon this question ; and, failing that, at all events, reserving to the people of this country the power at some future time to take over this undertaking and work it for the general advantage of the people of Canada as a whole. This proposal differs from the ordinary remedy of expropriation in this particular, that usually it is the case of the government, or of some large corporation, taking over property that absolutely belongs to another, but in this case we take over a property in which the company is interested to the extent of about 10 per cent, and in which the country is interested to the extent of about 90 per cent. We are the sole owners of the eastern division, and as to the western division, I am safe in saying that we contribute at least 75 per cent of the entire expenditure, so that I am probably correct in saying that Canada has invested 90 per cent of the entire money required for this huge project. The necessity for expropriation has become very manifest during the progress of this debate. Let me say right here that I think I can, with very great show of reason, adopt the language used by the Prime Minister when he introduced this measure, and say that the proposals in this amendment are so fair and reasonable in themselves ; so manifestly in the interests of the country, that I can appeal, even at this late hour, with some degree of confidence, to the government and their supporters to take this matter into their favourable consideration and adopt . the amendment.
X need hardly remind old parliamentarians that this is not. a new system of legislation, that provision for expropriation was included in the old Act of Incorporation of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and that in a number of statutes passed In Canada in earlier times, provision for expropriation by the government was inserted. It is true that in later years we have not adopted this method, but having regard to the fact that in all the lighter railway enterprises in England and in the matter of tramways, provisions of this kind occur, and in the light of the fact that every day the tendency towards government ownership is developing and becoming more pronounced, I think that the time has evidently come when, in connection with a new undertaking
such as this, there is good reason to ask the government when granting such large concessions to this company to accept the amendment which I now propose. I do not distinguish between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, because in this regard I entirely adopt the language of the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) of last session. There is one company to all intents and purposes; as he was forced to admit it is the same red-headed boy. I say that when we reflect that the company we are dealing with is a company whose interests are antagonistic to the interests of the people of Canada, a company whose interests in the east as well as in the west are identified with the interests of the United States, a company whose chief official, as far as management is concerned, is a man whose interests are identified in a very pronounced way with the interests of the United States, when we reflect that we are dealing practically with a foreign corporation it is clearly in the interests of the people of Canada that this provision should be made. It is necessary also in the interests of the people of the west. The speech in which the right hon. gentleman who leads the House introduced this measure last session, although he would like to have it forgotten, has not been forgotten. The urgency that he portrayed on that occasion has not been lost sight of by the people of the country, although it has been lost sight of in the amendments introduced this session. In order that we shall have, not what the government propose to give us now-the possibility of a railway being constructed in the west within eight years-in order that we shall have what the government promised us a year ago -the rapid construction of this railway for the purpose of easing the congestion of the west, of bringing relief to the people of the west and providing for the every day increasing resources of that great territory, and in order that we shall have the prompt and speedy construction of that railway it is necessary, I believe, that we should have the provision which I have taken this opportunity to move. If anything is required to emphasize the fact that both the Railway Companies and the government have come to a complete halt in this matter, it is found in the fact not only that the government have extended the time for an additional period of three ' years, nearly doubling the time originally given, but in the fact that the railway company have found it necessary to make a special provision in regard to leasing a portion of the line showing, what probably the government do not desire to admit, that it is not contemplated either on the part of the company or the government that there shall be a rapid construction of this line such as was proclaimed by the right hon. the leader of the government, when he introduced his measure last session.

Therefore, I say that there is a necessity for adopting this measure in order that we shall have some method of taking over such portion of the railway as may be completed, and to enable us to carry out and implement the policy announced by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) last year that we propose in the immediate future to carry to the people of the west the relief they require and give to the people who are going into that country abundant facilities for transporting their produce from their homes to the markets of the world. It is a necessity also that we should adopt this method in order to safeguard that great national asset the Intercolonial Railway. We have invested our money in that enterprise. This government since their advent in 1896 have been spending large sums of money upon that railway. We have come to the position now that the Intercolonial Railway, while not exactly a remunerative investment in a direct sense, yet affords special facilities to the people down by the sea and having been placed upon a splendid basis of equipment, has arrived at the period when it is practically a concern paying its own way. Therefore, we are met at this, a most unfortunate time, by the government proposing to sacrifice that work by the construction of the eastern division of this Transcontinental Railway. As a matter of safeguarding and protecting the Intercolonial Raiway which is a great national asset we are also justified in adopting the measure I have introduced. I also urge it as a means of checking the reckless extravagance which is announced by the government in the matter of pushing that line down to Moncton. If this measure is adopted and if we have these expropriation powers, there will be yet time to prevent the government from going on with such a reckless waste of money as to push the line from Quebec to Moncton. But, above and beyond all this, above and beyond the mere question of money, and I do feel that there has been a most recklessly extravagant bargain made by the government, that they have utterly failed to safeguard the interests of the people, there is one matter that is of greater and of more far reaching importance and that is the question of securing a national highway such as that proclaimed by the right hon. gentleman who leads the government-of making this in fact as well as1 in a name a national highway. I therefore, in introducing this amendment, have in mincT that whatever waste of money there may be-and there inevitably will be, I suppose, a waste of money by the manner in which the government have proceeded with this work, the provision which I introduce is the only remedy now left us by which we can secure what the right hon. gentleman promised when he introduced this measure, namely, the transportation of Canadian pro-Mr. LENNOX.
duce across Canadian territory and through Canadian ports.
This has practically been abandoned by the government during the discussion of this1 matter. They have practically abandoned the contention of last session that there is any means by which we can compel this railway to be in any true sense a national highway. They have practically abandoned the contention that we can, by any means which lie within the four corners of this statute or this contract, compel the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk to carry our* produce to a Canadian shipping port. Therefore 1 say that important as the money question is, of transcendent importance is the question of controlling the transportation of this country across Canadian territory ; and whatever might have been done had the government adopted a wise policy in the beginning, there appears to be no remedy left now other than the adoption of the system which is provided for by the amendment now moved, namely, the taking control of this matter into our own hands, and thus preventing any diversion of our traffic to American territory. We need this also as a means of expressing and enforcing the people's will. It has always been understood by the people of this country-for they understand the theory of responsible government-that any new departure, any great measure involving a question of policy, must be submitted to the people for their approval before it is adopted by parliament. On this occasion, the parliament of Canada, have seen fit to ignore this practice. The government saw fit last session to tell us that by reason of the immediate necessity of the case, the urgency that existed, they would have to dispense with that practice, and put this measure through without submitting it to the people. I hope by means of the amendment which I have moved to give the people an opportunity, late as it will be, of pronouncing on this question as soon as the government dares to submit the matter to the people. I hope, in common with others of the Conservative party, to hold out to the people that there is yet a chance of having their voice heard at the polls, and of undoing partially, though not completely, the wrongs committed by the government in connection with this contract. For these reasons I thmk we have good grounds for submitting these amendments to the consideration of the House. If the matter stood as it did last session, there would be abundant reasons for saying that there should be an appeal to the people ; but, bad as the contract was last year, it is more than doubly bad to-day, owing to the amendments that have been made in it. You cannot take one clause of the amended contract and not find in it evidence of a complete surrender by the government of

the .interests of the people of Canada to the interests of the Grand Trunk Company. This is emphasized in almost every speech made in this House during this discussion by ministers of the Crown, who declared that they had to accept the terms dictated by the Grand Trunk Company. Looking at these amendments in the contract, we find the most glaring instances of the government surrendering not only everything the company asks, but in many instances more than they ask. Where last session we had $20,000,000 of rolling stock provided for, it is now reduced to $15,000,000. The guarantee of $5,000,000 which was to remain as security for the performance of every part of the contract is now to be released at an early stage and is only to form a security for the performance of a part of the contract by the company. The need for haste which was described in such graphic language by the right hon. leader of the government last session is now no longer in existence, but at the mere suggestion of the company three years are added to the time, even with regard to the prairie section, as to which at all events no excuse can be given for increasing the time. Additional concessions have been given to the company by the increase of our liability for the mountain section of from $8,010,000 to $10,000,000 so far as the guarantee is concerned, and an actual payment of .money to the extent of $2,000,000 ; and there is a complete collapse by the government, so far as the control of rates is concerned, and the control of the bonds provided for by last year's agreement. I do not want to quote again the language of the Minister of Finance ; but it is still fresh in our memory what he said last year about the control of rates that we would retain by reason of the fact that not one dollar of that stock should be disposed of by the Grand Trunk Pacific, that he had arranged with the Grand Trunk for the retention of that stock for the protection of the people of the country, and in order that the rates might be effectually controlled in the interest of the people. Yet with all these professions of a year ago, the government, as an additional misfortune for the people, have completely surrendered that protection -so far as it was any protection-whether in the matter of rates or in the general control of Canadian traffic through Canadian channels to Canadian ocean ports. Now, if there is anything that should add to the condemnation which I feel ought to be meted out to the government in regard to this measure, it is the time they selected for introducing this measure, and for forcing on the ipeople, unnecessarily, this great burden. It was just at the time when the Canadian Northern Railway had got into a position with added equipment, to control and handle a large portion of the trade of the west. It was a time when the government, by a large
expenditure, both upon our waterways and upon our government railway, had put our national highways in a position of comparative efficiency. It was a time when we had arrived at what is now called an era of government ownership, when the attention of the government ought to have been arrested by the fact that other countries, some of the most progressive, such as Germany, Italy, France, Belgium, Russia, Australia and South Africa, had all adopted the principle of government ownership-when government ownership was in the air-when the doctrine of government ownership of public utilities was being discussed in every part of Canada, and the people had expressed in no uncertain tone their desire < to have that principle introduced in * all our larg(e undertakings. It was at a time when the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) drew attention in a most specific manner to the importance of extending the Intercolonial to Georgian bay. and ultimately to the west, and at such a time it was the duty of the government, before committing themselves to the Grand Trunk Pacific, to have formed a policy on this question and submitted it to the people for their verdict. I therefore fefel that in proposing an amendment which will enable the government to take over the lines of railway on giving reasonable compensation-not allowing the companies to actually lose, but on the other hand not allow them to unduly profit-the opposition are doing their duty by the people. The adoption of such a measure will not offer a complete remedy because there will still be a large concession made to this company. We cannot escape serious loss in any event, but we should submit the question to the people, and if the people approve the policy, the government should hasten to give effect to their desire.

speechtext:
I would not attempt to address the House at this late hour were it not for the fact that a few days ago I proposed an amendment, and said I would move it on the third reading. It is now near mid night and the House is very thin, scarcely sufficient being present to make a quorum. I am strongly in favour of the amendment I moved a few days ago, which is on the same lines as the one now submitted by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). The amendment of the hon. member may be somewhat more elaborate than mine, drawn up in lawyer's style, and might perhaps be better understood, but since it contemplates government ownership, I think that the government should consider well the propriety of taking over this railway within ten years at least. But according to the argumeut it seems that the company will be allowed control a hundred years. Unless I am very much mistaken, the people will be sorry in-

deed if any government should have granted power to a corporation to run across our continent and treat us as they please without the government having the opportunity of taking over the road, so that they may have a competing road with the other two lines, one of which is already built and the other is being rapidly completed. No other government has ever had such an opportunity of showing the people that they are in earnest. What is the reason they do not embrace this opportunity ? Is it because the opposition have submitted the policy, and the government are determined not to accept any advice from this side of the House ' I think the government ought to consider this amendment, and if they will accept it there will he no need for me to move mine. In "any case 1 may as well drop my amendment, as if this does not carry, mine is sure to be thrown out. But these lion, gentlemen opposite who, when in opposition always held up both hands in favour of giving the people their rights now will not do anything except follow in the footsteps of previous administrations. It has been the custom of all governments, since time immemorial, to protect wealthy corporations. Since the days when Joseph cornered all the grain in Egypt, and since the days when Saul wTas king, a few people have always had the pull on the party in powTer. A few people have the pull now, and it is time that those people who are always professing sympathy for the public, should do something for them. How can they do it ? They can do it by having a provision inserted in the Bill which will give the government an opportunity of owning a railway across the continent. I do not expect that the government will accept the amendment. Should it be put to the vote, the House will fill up in a few minutes and men who have not heard the arguments and know nothing about the subject will vote against government ownership. Some people say that if we adopt this principle of government ownership it will lead to socialism. AVell, we own our canals, is that state socialism ? We own 1,500 miles of railway, have we ever had a complaint made that the government own such a railway ?
We carry all the mails through the country ; is that socialism ? We build public buildings in almost every town and city for the public benefit; is that socialism ? Whatever can be done in the interest of the people may be called socialism. Never mind what it is called, what's in a name ? What we want is a great highway across this continent to compete with these wealthy corporations to whom the government-other governments, not this government-have given away nearly all otir country-and now this government is following in the same footsteps. I have some further notes but I do not wish to take up the time of the House. All I would ask of the government is to consider this matter and see if they Mr. JABEL ROBINSON.
cannot insert a clause so that before sopie of us shuffle off this mortal coil, we may have the pleasure of seeing a railroad owned and worked by the people in the interests of the people across this great continent. I want to do what I think is for the best interest of my country, that is what we are here for ; if any man is here for anything else you had better pay him off as soon as you can-and there are plenty here, it seems to me, for something else. There are some individuals who think they ought to own not only the whole earth but everything that is on it and these men who are trying to make the government help them are just that class of individuals. They want to own the soil, they want to own the whole country and make us pay tribute. Europe is owned by a few individuals, the United Kingdom is owned by a few individuals. And how do they own it ? Just by monopolies starting in early days just as these are being created to-day and as others have been created within the last thirty years in this country. We are going to have this country owned by a few men in very short order if we insist on carrying out the schemes whereby we are now trying to develop the country. It is aristocracy and moneyoeracv that is going to rule and the people who have votes will have nothing to say about it because they will always vote straight party every time and will never vote for the interest of the country. While there are two strong parties as we have to-day whichever party is in power will get these corporations to contribute the money for them and will so be able to carry the country. I am not speaking for or against one party or the other but we know that to be the fact. It is going to be the same next time ?
