I rise simply to assure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fitzpatrick) that we are greatly disappointed. I might go further and venture the statement that the people of Canada will be greatly disappointed at the airy manner in which the hon. gentleman has waved this important amendment aside. The hon. gentleman has lost sight of the fact, whether he has forgotten it or not, that this is a question involving great considerations to the people of Canada. It is a flat refusal on the part of the hon. gentlemen and the government of which he is so distinguished a member to permit the people to express themselves upon such a grave question as this. I would ask the right hon. gentleman who leads the House if he feels that he is warranted in asking his supporters in this House, at the end of a parliament constituted as this parliament is, to assent to a measure involving such great considerations, one of the greatest measures ever presented before a parliament, without giving the people of the country a single opportunity to express themselves upon the question. What mandate has the right hon. gentleman or his government to ask the people to accept this measure and to tell them afterwards :	It
is all done, it was done by a majority of the representatives in this House and therefore you must accept it. I deny that the right hon. gentleman or his government has any right or mandate from the people to undertake a measure of the magnitude of this one. If at the time of the last election the people had had any intimation that a measure of even half the magnitude of this one was to be proposed it would be a fair thing to say that they had some warning. As it is they have no warning. The only answer I would expect to this criticism-because no better answer could be given worthless as in my judgment that answer would be-is the excusing question :	Can Canada afford to
pass an Act of this kind and put a clause of repudiation in that Act when passing it ? I say the peojjle of Canada have rights just as well as any great corporation in Canada. The people of Canada should be treated in the same manner as any great and wealthy corporation should be treated. What has been the history of this matter ? The Right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said it was a matter of life and death that this matter should be taken up and pressed through to a thorough consummation at the earliest prssible moment.
A solemn contract was made and confirmed by a vote of a majority of this House, but I
am glad to say very much against the will of the minority, and I believe much against the will of a majority, of the people, who had not been consulted. What followed Y After that - contract was signed, sealed, and delivered, within six or seven months, that corporation came back, not to the people of Canada I am sorry to say-because the people of Canada had no opportunity to speak, the government not being disposed to allow them a voice in the question-they came back to the government and said :	We absolutely repudiate
every line we put our hands to on a former occasion ; give us better terms or we will throw up the whole thing. Should the people of Canada be accused of repudiation or of action that would tarnish the credit or the. honour of the country, even if they were to put a clause of this kind in this Bill, so that this company and all the world might understand, that the people of Canada do not feel themselves more bound than the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific felt themselves bound a few months ago ? No. This contract is pregnant with the most important issues ever brought to theattention of any parliament of Canada. The case is one exceptional in every way.
I venture the statement, and, I am confident, without danger of successful contradiction, that in the whole history of railway building on the continent of America, and I might go further and say, in the whole history of railway building in the world, no parallel case can be found to this. Here is a government entering deliberately into partnership with a great corporation. They are doing more-they are sacrificing every single interest of the people of Canada affected by this contract. They surrendered everything to the demands of the corporation, yet I defy hon. gentlemen opposite to point out a single concession that has been given in return for all the concessions that we are granting. Now, without prolonging this debate which, I see, is perfectly useless

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Some hon. gentleman says ' certainly.' Surely it cannot be my hon. friend from Victoria (Hon. Wm. Ross), a prominent member of this House, a gentleman who occupied a responsible position in former days under a distinguished leader of the Liberal party whose record, upon the whole, is a creditable one, and who, I am sure, would never have supported a transaction of this kind. I am sure that if my hon. friend (Hon. Wm. Ross) were to follow the dictates of his conscience at this moment he would not support this contract. There is no man with his sense of honour or appreciation of the duty belonging to his position but must feel a desire to repudiate every line of this contract which he is now forced, by his loyalty to his party-and, 1 was going to say. by want of loyalty to his country-to support.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: We will hear what the country has to say about it by and by.	.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman from Victoria think of applying that rule in private life-for the agent to bind his principal to a bargain which that principal would not approve and then defy him to undo it or change it V If the hon. gentleman Is in earnest in what he says-and 1 believe he is-let him vote for the proposition of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox). He will then give the people some means of speaking and speaking effectively. But the friends of the hon. gentleman seek to muzzle the people and then defy them to tear up this contract. I thought when my hon. friend said ' certainly,' that is was a cry of despair, because the hon. gentleman knew perfectly well that the majority would pass the measure quite irrespective of its merits. I repeat that I know of no occasion when it was more clearly the duty of the leader of a great party to give the people the right to declare themselves upon a public question instead of passing the measure and telling the country that the thing is done and they might as well make the best of it. That is practically the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I listened with care to the-what shall I call it ? well-the speech, of my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy). It was sentimental ; I do not wish to qualify it with any adjective. But I doubt that the hon. gentleman has read the amendment or listened to the speech of his neighbour who moved it or of the hon. gentleman who seconded it. He spoke as though the amendment were to keep the contract in suspension until it had been referred to the people, and a declaration that we should not bind the people until the people had an opportunity to pass upon this question. That is not the tenor of this amendment. It is simply to provide that the government should take power to expropriate the railway at some future day.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman so understands it ? Then, he will permit me to say, it is impossible to understand the tenor of the comments he has made upon it. I will have a civil answer to give the hon. gentleman and one to satisfy his conscience if it can be satisfied, that the position he has taken is absolutely without foundation. The right of expropriation is a paramount right of the government.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I know that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
Then, if that is the case, there is no necessity for this amendment. To-day this parliament has power to expropriate the Canadian Racittc Railway ; we have power to expropriate the ' Mr. CLANCY.
Grand Trunk-and we are advised every day to do it. We have power to expropriate the telegraph and telephone companies, and we are advised every day to exercise that power. When the charters were given to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway and to the various telegraph and telephone companies no restriction was put upon the government's power to expropriate them, a right which, as I say is inherent in the government. If we were prepared to accept a new doctrine for the Conservative party, to adopt the policy toward which they are going-or, rather, I should say, towards which they are pushed by some agitators on their own side-we could use the power we have to expropriate all these companies. But we do not believe in that. Should there be, in the future, a government of Canada that wishes to expropriate the railways and administer them for the benefit-or the injury-of the state, it will always be in their power to do so, whether this amendment is passed or not.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Will the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) permit me to ask him a question ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
Does not he see that that amendment would become a portion of the contract, and, whereas we have the right to expropriate in every ease, we would, in this case, have that right by contract, and, if we exercised it nobody could say we exercised it unfairly ?
Sir- WILFRID LAURIER. Nobody could say we exercised it unfairly at any time. But if this government or any government were to adopt the policy of government ownership, it should adopt it With regard to all companies and not with regard to one company only.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: But there is this difference. We are assisting fo build a very expensive railway, providing for it about nine dollars out of every ten. The time when we are giving that assistance would be the proper time, I should imagine, to lay down the principle of taking that railway at some future time, if we desire to do so. The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says we have the power to expropriate. It is true we have that power. But it is also true that we have not yet exercised it. But, with the growing sentiment of the country in favour of government ownership, and with the large sum we are paying for this railway, it seems proper that we should lay down the principle as part of the contract that we may take the road back in the future if we desire to do so, and upon what terms. If that were done, and the company accepted the assistance upon that condition, it could not be said that any injustice was done, if we took back the railway upon these lines.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, X wish to say one word as to the observation made by the right hon. gentleman who leads the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in regard to the right of expropriation. The right hon. gentleman seems to think that the Grand Trunk Railway Com pany and other companies were incorporated without any right of expropriation. If he will look at the statutes incorporating the Great Western Railway Company and old companies afterwards forming the Grand Trunk Company, he will find that they contained provisions almost identical with that which has been moved by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). The Great Western Railway Company's Act of Incorporation certainly had that provision, and I know that several other railways that were incorporated at that time had a provision in their charters enabling the government to expropriate the property and take it over.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Since confederation ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: It was before confederation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: That may be. I do not dispute that.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: One of the reasons for that practice was that in the early days of railways it was supposed that they could be treated as public highways. That became an absurdity, and the public came to think that it would not be possible or expedient at any time for the government to own railways, and so such clauses were omitted in later statutes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: There has been a change, and a very , great change, in public opinion since those days, and probably we will come back before long to the old-fashion of putting in every charter a provision such as that which it is proposed to put into this Bill. That is, that there should be the express power of expropriation. If you have a charter without express terms as to expropriation, the owners of a property may claim from arbitrators very much higher compensation than could reasonably be claimed if they took their charter with the express provision that their property was subject to expropriation. That is just the object of this amendment, and the whole of the terms of the resolution proposed by my hon. friend from South .Simcoe point to that very thing. You will find in the tramway Acts and other similar corporation Acts in England the like provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: It is contained in the general law.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
Yes, there is that same right as to all of them. The right hon. leader of the government says that you have the
right of expropriation without any express provision ; and so he asks why put it in this Act, if you have it already ? The object is to let everybody who takes stock in the corporation know before hand that the property is subject to expropriation. Everybody will understand that when arbitrators are asked to fix the value of a property owned by people who knew when they acquired it that it was expressly subject to expropriation they will not allow such damages or compensation as would be given to persons who entered into a speculation having no notice or knowledge that the property was subject to expropriation. That is the ground upon which this resolution is moved.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: That is all specially provided for.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
And it is for this reason that the hon. gentleman made provision in regard to running powers. Although he had the right to take running powers over this road, the hon. gentleman made the same provision with regard to running powers over the western section.
Amendment (Mr. Lennox) negatived on the same division.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution proposed by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), and which has now been disposed of, is one that perhaps may be termed sweeping in this, that almost before this company has commenced their operations the government of the day might intervene and take possession of the road under the expropriation clause proposed. I propose to move an amendment, under which the right of expropriation may be exercised upon the happening of certain contingencies, and after I have read the resolution it will be seen that the contingencies anticipated in this regard are the same that have been dwelt upon at great length in the course of this debate. One of the strongest reasons advanced for the construction of this line of railway has been that it would be purely and essentially a Canadian system, and that we would have the advantage in years to come of seeing all the trade of the west pouring through Canadian territory and finding an outlet through Canadian ports. I therefore beg to move this resolution, seconded by Mr. Armstrong :
That the Bill he not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions to add the following section thereto :-
(1)	In case the government after due inquiry and investigation is satisfied at any time that the Pacific Company is not, or that the Grand Trunk Company in controlling the policy of the Pacific Company is not fairly and honestly carrying out and performing the covenants, stipulations and agreements in the 41st, 42nd, 43rd, 44th and 45th clauses of the original agreement contained, or that traffic is not being routed by but is being directed from Canadian channels

and Canadian ports, it shall be lawful for the government at any time thereafter upon six months' notice to the Pacific Company to expropriate, acquire and take over the whole undertaking, railways, branch lines, terminals, ap-purtenaces, rolling stock, equipment, hereditaments and real and personal property of the Pacific Company, including the unexpired term of the lease of the eastern division, but not including moneys, securities for moneys and choses in action, and to own and operate the said railways and branch lines and other property.
(2)	Immediately upon the expiration of six months from the date of service of such notice upon the Pacific Company, the government may enter into possession of and the Pacific Company shall deliver to the government possession of the said railways, branch lines,1 terminals, appurtenances, rolling stock, equipment, hereditaments, and real and personal property.
(3)	If in such case the government and the Pacific Company shall fail to agree upon the amount of compensation to be paid to the Pacific Company for the property so expropriated, acquired and taken over by the government, the same shall be determined by arbitrators to be appointed in the manner provided in the 47th clause of the original agreement.
(4)	The arbitrators in considering, arriving at and making their award? shall have regard to and take into account the following matters :-
(a.) No allowance shall be made or sum awarded for or on the basis of past or future profits or earning powers or by way of good will or upon any speculative basis or for disappointment, or by reason of the sale being compulsory, and the gross amount to be allowed or credited to the Pacific Company before taking into account deductions and sums of money to be retained, shall not in any case exceed the actual value of the property taken over, having regard to and on the basis of the matters immediately hereinbefore provided for.
(b.) Account shall be taken of the total amount of all payments, outlays and contributions by the government whether as money, land, interest paid without recourse, or otherwise on account or in connection with the property taken over, and the gross sum otherwise payable by the government, shall in addition to any other deduction to be made be reduced in the proportion which this sum bears to the total cost of the property taken over. Such total cost shall be based upon and shall include the original cost of construction as defined in the scheduled agreements, together with any subsequent expenditure (not being working expenditure) upon capital account for betterments.
(c.) The arbitrators shall take an account of all bonds, mortgages and debts constituting a charge upon the property taken over and also of the amount of the liability of the government for the Pacific Company by guarantees or otherwise, and the government shall thereupon be taken to have assumed direct liability as between the government and the Pacific Company for the payment of all these debts, charges and liabilities, and to have undertaken to indemnify the Pacific Company from liability or action, and this being done the total amount of these debts, charges and liabilities so ascertained shall by the award be set off against or deducted from the sum of money otherwise payable to the Pacific Company, and the bal-Mr. BENNETT.
ance shall be awarded to be paid by the government to the Pacific Company, or by the company to the government, as the case may be, with interest at per cent from the date of taking possession.
(5)	The government shall not exercise the said power of expropriating and acquiring the said undertaking, railways, branch lines and other property of the Pacific Company unless and until parliament shall have first made provision by an Act or Acts to be passed in that behalf for authorizing the raising and payment of the compensation to-be awarded by the arbitrators as aforesaid.
In support of this amendment dealing with the question of expropriation, I cannot add much to what has been said by the mover and seconder of the preceding resolution, but I have just this to say, that I quite agree that if the country is to have any opportunity of pronouncing upon this proposal, involving as it does such a huge expenditure, if such a resolution is passed it will have this effect that should there be a change of government, or even if there should not be, this company will have their eyes wide open as to the terms and conditions upon which this charter has been granted. In the province of Ontario this question of government and municipal ownership is a very live question ; in fact, ;t has been exercised to a very great extent in the cities _and towns in reference to gas plants, waterworks and electric light works, and so strong has been the feeling in that regard that we have now in Ontario legislation which prevents any corporation from engaging in the business of establishing electric plants, waterworks or gasworks, where there are existing going concerns Another reason that strongly prevails in Ontario in* favour of government ownership is the fact that most of the railways throughout the province have been largely subsidized and bonused by municipal corporations. These bonuses have, in a good many cases, been received from municipalities, and seeing that these railway companies are now paying very well and doing a profitable business, the .large bonuses which they have received in past years, as it were, come to naught. Had these companies been organized by the municipalities, or placed upon a business footing under government or municipal ownership, the municipalities to-day, taking into account what they have paid out, would have practically owned them. I would accentuate what has been said by other gentlemen, that while under the general law the government may at any time expropriate for public purposes, still it would be hardly fair to the company to take advantage of that. It would be much fairer that this condition be incorporated in the charter, so that investors might have before their eyes the fact that at any time the government of the day could exercise the privilege granted in this amendment. I beg to move the amendment, seconded by Mr. Armstrong.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
This Mr. Speaker, is one of the roost important amendments which have been proposed during the discussion. I think you will agree with me, Sir, that it will provide a safeguard for the people in reference to the shipment of our western trade over the Grand Trunk Pacific and through Canadian ports rather than through foreign ports. The government propose that the Grand Trunk Pacific shall develop trade through Canadian channels, but it does not impose a penalty if said trade is not carried to Canadian ports. This amendment places a penalty on the Grand Trunk Pacific if the trade is not directed to Canadian ports. We are not asking to take an unfair ad* vantage of the Grand Trunk Pacific. We are not asking the government of this country to do anything that will not be for the best interests of the people of this whole country. We are asking the representatives of the people of our land to assist in placing on our statute-book legislation that will prevent trouble in future.
There is not a man in this House who wants to see the trade of our great west go to a foreign port. We all believe in Canada for the Canadians, then let us guard the rights of our country with zealous care. Let us not take any chances of our trade being diverted to foreign channels. If our people have to pay the bulk of what it takes to build this road, surely we should have a right to demand that its operation will be conducted in our interests.
The members on this side of the House have presented some 25 amendments to the original contract, every one of which if accepted, would be in the interests of the people of this country. This amendment is one of the most important, for without it the traffic may be diverted to foreign ports, while with it we hold the reins of poweir. Let us in this contract make the meaning of it so plain that a wayfaring man though a fool, could not mistake the meaning of the words therein. Let us call a spade a spade, with regard to every line and every syllable of it, and let us not leave to future generations any doubt as to the meaning of every word in this contract. Clause 1 of the amendment states that if the Grand Trunk Pacific does not fairly and honestly carry out and perform the covenants, stipulations and agreements containtd in clauses 41. 42, 43. 44 and 45 of the original contract, or if traffic is being routed in an unfair and dishonest manner, to a foreign port, when it should have been carried over the Grand Trunk Pacific to St. John and Halifax ; it will then be the privilege and the duty of the 'government of this country to assume the whole undertaking. If I understand this question aright, the proposed Grand Trunk Pacific is being built for the benefit of the people of this country. There is not
a man in this House who will dare to vote one penny towards the building of this road if he cannot satisfy the people of his constituency that the trade will be carried through Canadian ports.
Clause 2 gives the government of this country power to take over the road by giving the Grand Trunk Pacific 6 months notice, and proving by Act of parliamnt that the Grand Trunk Pacific is not complying with the contents of clauses mentioned. The 3rd and 4th clauses of the amendment provides for the appointment of arbitrators and stipulates the course they are to pursue. Clause 5 refers to the duties of parliament with reference to the measure. Every clause in the amendment is safeguarding the people's rights, while not imposing any unfair demand on the Grand Trunk Pacific. I hope the hon. gentlemen opposite will see the justice of our claim and allow this amendment to become law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: The amendment means that the government, one of the parties to this contract, would have the right to investigate the conditions unuer which the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the other party, is operating the scheme ; and if on this ex parte investigation the government came to the conclusion that there is a failure on the part of the company to comply with the conditions of tile contract, the government has the right to enter into possession. In terms, the amendment is that one party to the contract is to be a law unto himself as to what the obligations of the other party are. Would any reasonable man in this House enter into a contract with such a clause in it, if he were honest and sincere in proposing to carry its terms out ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Is there not an exceptional condition in this contract, inasmuch as the one party supplies a very large proportion of the funds which will build the road ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: My hon. friend is confounding two things that ought to be kept apart. The money is provided by the aid of the credit of the government, as well as the aid of the credit of the Grand Trunk Company. If the contract is a success, the money is not to be paid by the government, but by the railway company. If a man endorses a note to enable his neighbour to get money, and if the neighbour pays, the endorser does not have to pay. What does the hon. gentleman mean by the question ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: If the Minister of Justice wishes me to reply. I would state that as regards the larger part of this railway we finance it out and out and pay for it, and as regards the other part we are liable for three-fourths of its cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: We finance the eastern division and build it, and own it; that we cannot expropriate. So far as the western division is concerned the road is constructed and financed by the joint action of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the government, and the party to the contract who pays for it is the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the government are the parties to the contract, and this amendment is intended to give the government the right to determine whether or not the Grand Trunk has fulfilled its share of the agreement. If the government, one of the parties to the agreement comes to the conclusion that the other party is not fulfilling the conditions of the agreement, then the government would have the right to refer the matter to arbitration.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: The hon. minister will remember that in the motion of the hou. member for South Simcoe, as well as in the one which I proposed, as a condition precedent parliament must supply the funds in the event of an arbitration being held ; so that there is not only the other party interested, the government of the day, but also parliament itself as an appeal court, and as having to provide the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: There is no use of confounding the government and parliament. In effect, what is the difference between the two ? The government is only a committee appointed by parliament to carry on the work of the country.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: But there is the intervention of parliament, which is not supposed to be so hide-bound that it will perpetrate a wrong upon a party irrespective of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Why lay down a principle that a wrong may be done ? I can understand the preceding amendment, because it involves government ownership, that is to say, it gives legal effect in the contract to the constitutional right vested in the government of entering into possession of any government work. My hon. friend says there is a provision in England with respect to the government taking possession of tramways. The hon. gentleman is aware that under Sir Robert Peel's government a general law was introduced made applicable to all railways, which authorized the government, twenty years after a charter was granted, to enter into possession ; but has any effect ever been given to that law ? Never. I defy the hon. member for Hamilton to cite a single case.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I have no doubt some tramways have been taken over by the municipalities.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Not under the general law.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Yes, under the same provision. The county of London can take over tramways to-day under the provision of the General Acts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: My hon. friend, it seems to me, has entirely overlooked sections 41, 42 and 43, taken in conjunction with section 47. If there is a failure on the part of the company to perform any of its obligations under the contract, there is a reference to arbitration provided,' not a forcible entry.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: In the case of an arbitration under section 47, as to the routing of the traffic, and the arbitrators find against the company, what is the remedy ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
Failure as to the condition of the whole agreement.
Mr. BARKER, Some man whose goods were sent to Portland instead of Halifax might be asked what damages he should get.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: That is not the question. I would ask my hon. friend from East Simcoe as a business man whether he would enter into an agreement which would give the other party the right to determine whether he had fulfilled the conditions of the agreement or not ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is overlooking the fact that the First Minister has told us that parliament can expropriate without any clause. So that it is not extending the power further to say that we can do it for cause. The whole object of this clause is to give the parties due notice. That it may be on the face of the contract. The right hon. First Minister tells us that we can do it without any contract at all, and there is no doubt that we can. All we say is that the parties should take their charter and enter upon their work on the distinct understanding that this can be done, and that in the event of these clauses not being honestly observed and carried out, the remedy of the people of Canada will not be to seek some trifling damages, but to take the contract off their hands. That is the remedy we want to have.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: It seems to me that it is desirable for this reason, that the company assumes certain obligations, and in the event of their failing to carry out those obligations, there is no remedy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: I put it to my hon. friend as a fair-minded man, is it fair to give one party the right to determine whether the other party is fulfilling its obligations or not ?

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext: Tlie government which is furnishing the money to build the railway ought to have more rights than the company. In the absence of any penalty I think it is important that the government should have some greater right than it has, and that is provided for in the proposed amendment.

maintopic: ALIEN LABOUR LAW A DEAD LETTER.
speechtext:
This is a partnership matter, and the amendment only proposes to give the partner who has the larger share in the contract the greater right. The partner who has the larger share is the country, and the country should have the right to say through the vote of its representatives in parliament on their hono*ur whether or not this contract is being properly carried out. It will be found in the contract that there are certain instances in in which the decision is left to the Governor in Council ; it is not unfair that this matter should be left to the decision of the representatives of the people in parliament when the people have nine-tenths interest in the transaction. It is not, as the Minister of Justice says, a one-sided matter, left to one of the contracting parties. There is a substantial difference between the parliament and the government. The parliament is supposed to have the interest of the country at heart and it represents the Grand Trunk as well as the other people of Canada, so that I do not think there is anything unfair in this proposition. It is however rather refreshing to find that the government have so little to say on important subjects, and yet cavil over small matters. They did not discuss the main question involved in the amendment just disposed of, but, evading the issue, the right hon. gentleman urged that we have already the right of expropriation, but that is not what we are asking for. We are asking for contractual rights. We are not yet committed to the Grand Trunk Railway beyond redemption and are endeavouring to save the people from the clutches of that company. The Minister of Justice said he would not allow the hon. member for "West Toronto to escape him. Well, what we are asking is that he should allow the people to escape to some extent from the Grand Trunk Railway, and we can do this if we embody the amendment proposed in the agreement.
Amendment (Mr. Bennett) negatived on the same division.
